anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>Consider a hypothetical scenario in which an online shopping platform has become extremely successful. It has outgrown its original database. This causes order histories to load very slowly. Maintenance takes much longer than it used to. And engineers spend way too much time managing the workload and the system’s limitations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The engineering team behind this system wants to replace the database and migrate the data to a new database that promises better performance. But you cannot take a popular online store offline to make the switch. Customers are always placing orders, changing addresses, and requesting refunds. The shop can’t be shut down just like that.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This scenario offers a glimpse of the main challenge inherent in production migrations. How do you change a working system while still running the service that people depend on? At scale, copying existing data during such migrations can take days. Also, many supporting applications may depend on the component being replaced. Every intermediate step needs to work while ordinary business continues.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we will look at how migrations work at scale and the key strategies that can help make it as efficient as possible.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: WorkOS makes sure auth, for your app and your agents, is never one of them.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong>In this episode</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why is the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ea5b1c3a-fd1a-402e-91d0-388ec2cf5e91?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>“grill-me” skill</span></a><span> so popular, and why does its creator swear by the importance of software fundamentals? </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/22a09911-9054-467d-b8f3-b299e4ece311?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Matt Pocock</span></a><span> created this widely-used skill – and many others – alongside being an educator, content creator, and engineer. His latest course is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/15169f91-5cb7-45b4-bf9d-97748714aabe?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>AI Hero</span></a><span>, and he previously created the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cdc5303b-db52-4118-913e-6453f16b1a55?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Total TypeScript</span></a><span> course that generated more than $2.5 million in total sales.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this episode, Matt and I discuss his unconventional path from working as a voice teacher to becoming a developer and going all-in on technical education. He reveals how communication skills helped him break into tech, why he took an unusual three-days-a-week contract at Vercel, and how he built Total TypeScript through workshops, courses, and lots of free tutorials.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We also explore “strategic coding,” and how he uses skills like “grill me” and “wayfinder” to plan, delegate, and course-correct with AI agents. Matt explains his “day shift” and “night shift” approach, why splitting context up can keep agents in their “smart zone,” and how concepts from classic software engineering books can guide agents to do better. In this episode, there’s also local versus cloud workflows, whether agents need TDD, how AI is changing the ways that engineers learn the fundamentals, and why humans are still essential in teaching.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong>Takeaways from the conversation with Matt</strong></h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/630507e7-f225-495d-8815-2c2a605e7c87?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/4DhcSPkEbwI" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. Matt hacked together a web app for students while working as a voice coach. </span></strong><span>He taught himself JavaScript to build a web audio spectrogram analyzer for singing students, while he was teaching singing, accents, and Shakespeare at drama schools. He also ran his own company at university, studied for a Master’s qualification in voice, and coached consulting firms on public speaking.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Matt took a Vercel job in case Total TypeScript did not work out.</span></strong><span> Matt produced a lot of two-minute TypeScript tip videos which became popular. When he received a fulltime job offer from Vercel, Matt negotiated to work three days per week as a contractor so he could develop his TypeScript course on the other days. When it took off, Matt quit Vercel to focus entirely on his educational projects.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. Matt does not work on weekends and dislikes the concept of ‘9-9-6.’ </span></strong><span>He explained that everything he does is an effort to build a lifestyle where he can spend most of his time with his family. That’s the goal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>4. The  ‘grill-me’ skill was inspired by from Anthropic’s Thariq Shihipar. </span></strong><span>The grill-me skill is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/09ff1c42-a864-4e1a-8b0a-8683d62e5cba?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>surprisingly simple and short</span></a><span>: it instructs an agent to interview the user relentlessly. Thariq shared his approach of an agent interviewing its user about a topic – and how it was surprisingly useful –, and Matt created a skill around the novel concept.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>5. Is “strategic programming” the future of devs’ work? </span></strong><span>Borrowing from John Ousterhout’s “tactical programming” vs “strategic programming” categorization, Matt believes that agents are more than capable of tactical programming, leaving us engineers to spend more time at the “strategic” level.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>6. Using the right “leading words” makes agents produce better results. </span></strong><span>Matt noticed that agents try to build software layer by layer and that this causes bugs between the layers. Reading The Pragmatic Programmer, he discovered the concept of a “tracer bullet.” When he instructed the agent to use “tracer bullets” to build an app (aka implement a “golden path”), the agent started to produce better code! Since then, Matt has started reading classic software engineering books to discover other “leading words” that guide agents efficiently.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>7. Cloud-based agent setups make more sense than running agents locally. </span></strong><span>Matt is moving his coding sessions to cloud agents because doing so means agents run when he closes his laptop and cloud agents can be made “multiplayer” (collaborative) in ways that local agents cannot.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>8. Memento-driven development: optimize your codebase for a colleague who wakes up with no memory every morning.</span></strong><span> Matt says:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Imagine you have a human who wakes up every morning and cannot remember who they are, like the guy from Memento. We are trying to optimize our codebases for new starters, so we want the healthiest codebase we’ve ever had. A human can work around a bad codebase and they develop a memory about it, but an agent can’t do that; it starts afresh every single session. So, you need to optimize your codebase for that agent. And it turns out that software fundamentals have been trying to do that [optimize codebases for readability/understandability for someone who sees the code for the first time] for the entire time.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>9. Matt has mixed feelings on Test-Driven Development (TDD) with agents. </span></strong><span>He believes TDD is helpful for devs as we tend to have shorter working memories, and so a failing test will remind a distracted human of what is still failing. However, agents have longer context windows, so Matt has started to ask agents to produce proof that their code works – with or without TDD. </span><em><span>We cover another take on TDD in our </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8bde43b5-1363-4019-ba42-fc475f88d264?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>episode with Kent Beck.</span></a></em></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro something odd. Was it the prompt, a tool call that timed out, or a response your code could not parse? Without traces, you are guessing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this hands-on workshop, Serge from Sentry instruments three agents with Sentry Agent Tracing: a chatbot in an ecommerce store, a custom Slack agent, and a GitHub Action that reviews PRs. You will see how to catch bad tool calls and unexpected output, plus how to track token spend and performance across every agent you run.</span></p><p class="button-wrapper" data-attrs="{"url":"https://go.bytebytego.com/Sentry_091626","text":"Save your spot","action":null,"class":null}" data-component-name="ButtonCreateButton" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button primary" href="https://substack.com/redirect/40fa9785-2b6e-4d16-b340-6f71eb778141?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border: none;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;margin: 0;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;color: #ffffff !important;text-decoration: none !important;background-color: #7756e3;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><span style="color: #ffffff;text-decoration: none;">Save your spot</span></a></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Imagine a scenario where an employee is stranded at an airport after a cancelled flight. Before booking a hotel, they ask the company’s AI assistant a simple question: “Can I expense a hotel if my flight gets cancelled?”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The company has thousands of documents covering travel, expenses, insurance, employee benefits, and regional policies. Somewhere inside them, a paragraph states that accommodation costs caused by involuntary travel disruption are reimbursable, subject to certain conditions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For an LLM chatbot, finding that piece of information is harder than it appears. The question mentions a “cancelled flight,” while the policy refers to “involuntary travel disruption.” Other documents discuss hotels but apply to different countries. An older policy may be present that contains a reimbursement limit that has since changed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In such a case, the LLM must find information that matches the question’s meaning, belongs to the correct policy, and remains valid today. Only then can it write a useful answer that solves the user’s problem.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is known as the retrieval problem behind many LLM applications. In this article, we are going to look at how LLMs can find a needle in a haystack. Here’s what we will cover:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>An LLM needs evidence to answer questions</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The LLM Needs Evidence to Answer Questions</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A language model does not automatically know what is inside a company’s private documents. An application must provide that information, either by including documents directly in its input or by retrieving relevant passages when a question arrives.</span></p><div collection, retrieval offers a way to select a manageable amount of information. An embedding model converts the question into a numerical representation. A search system then uses that representation to find promising passages. The application supplies the original text to the LLM.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The model can then use those passages to explain the policy and cite the exact sources where it got the information from. This pattern is called retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG. A vector database supports the retrieval part by storing and searching numerical representations of content.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: responsibilities is really useful. If the application retrieves an outdated policy, even a capable language model will produce an outdated answer. If it retrieves a general hotel-booking rule while missing the cancellation exception, the answer may sound reasonably correct while overlooking the important condition.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Reliable answers therefore depend on what happens before generation. This means we have to make the document collection searchable at the right level of detail.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Documents are Turned into Searchable Passages</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A travel handbook can cover flights, accommodation, meals, approvals, and insurance. However, treating the entire handbook as a single searchable item produces a broad representation that can obscure a specific rule.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Instead, the application divides documents into smaller units called chunks. One chunk might describe hotel reimbursement, while another explains approval requirements. Search can then identify a particular passage instead of merely identifying the handbook that contains it.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Chunking creates a balance between precision and context. A small chunk may focus tightly on the question but leave out an exception. A large chunk may preserve the exception while including several unrelated policies. For example, suppose a passage says, “Accommodation expenses are reimbursable following a cancellation.” And the next sentence adds, “This applies only when accommodation is not provided by the airline.” Separating those sentences could cause the assistant to give an incorrect answer despite having the relevant text.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A useful chunk therefore preserves a complete idea wherever possible. Section headings and limited overlap between neighboring chunks can help retain context. The goal is to create passages that remain understandable when retrieved independently.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For our example question by the employee, the ideal searchable unit contains the reimbursement rule, its conditions, and enough identifying context to establish which policy it belongs to.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How LLMs Find the Meaning Behind Different Words</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Embeddings make it possible to search for related meaning even when the wording differs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An embedding model takes a passage and produces a vector: a list of numbers, often containing hundreds or thousands of decimal values. Think of it as a map of text. Passages with related meanings occupy nearby positions. For example, a question about hotel expenses after a cancelled flight should appear closer to a travel-disruption policy than to instructions for resetting a password.</span></p><div column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/314bf6b0-0fe8-4038-8d39-a99a68e77234_3800x2024.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":776,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":319930,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/215151603?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F314bf6b0-0fe8-4038-8d39-a99a68e77234_3800x2024.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The real representation has many more dimensions than a physical map. Individual dimensions also don’t have simple labels such as “hotel,” “flight,” or “reimbursement.” Meaning is represented through patterns across the complete vector.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The trick is that the application embeds the question into the same space as the document chunks. This way, it can compare the question’s vector with stored vectors to identify nearby passages. Also, the query and document embeddings must come from compatible encoders. However, matching vector lengths alone doesn’t make two models compatible.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each searchable record also needs a connection to the original text. The vector helps locate a passage, but the LLM needs the words themselves to interpret the rule. Therefore, a record should connect an embedding with a chunk identifier, the passage text, or its location. Also, metadata such as document ID, section, effective date, and version are present. These fields can be stored together or across connected storage systems. Structured identifiers make it possible to retrieve and maintain all chunks belonging to a document.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Close Is Close Enough?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The search system needs a precise definition of “nearby.” This definition comes from a distance or similarity metric, which compares two vectors and assigns a score. There are different metrics around this:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Cosine similarity compares their directions while ignoring their lengths.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Euclidean distance measures the straight-line distance between their endpoints, so vector length can influence the result.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Dot product reflects both alignment and length.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Normalization rescales vectors to length one. When both query and document vectors are normalized, dot product equals cosine similarity. Euclidean distance then produces the same ranking, although its scores differ. Dot product also works with unnormalized vectors when that matches the embedding model’s design.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The choice of the metric should follow the embedding model’s intended use. Choosing a metric simply because it is popular can change the ranking in unintended ways.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A similarity score should also be interpreted carefully. A score of 0.85 does not mean that a passage has an 85% probability of answering the question correctly. It describes a mathematical relationship between representations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The passage may discuss the right subject while stating the wrong regional policy. It may be outdated or omit an exception. Similarity provides evidence of relevance, but additional checks are needed before that evidence becomes an answer.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Why Searching Every Passage Is Too Expensive</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Searching every vector is straightforward, but the work grows with the collection.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/3d58f766-808e-40ed-bafe-063af5bb0a4b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/1d2609b5-c9f3-4ec7-8036-25272bd49f9b_3060x1450.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":690,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":221229,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/215151603?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1d2609b5-c9f3-4ec7-8036-25272bd49f9b_3060x1450.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A flat index compares the query with every eligible vector and returns those with the best scores. For a fixed number of dimensions, the comparison work grows roughly in proportion to the vector count. This is the meaning of O(n). If the collection doubles, the number of vector comparisons doubles. Longer vectors also require more work per comparison.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Flat search produces exact nearest neighbors under the selected metric. “Exact” describes the numerical search result. It doesn’t guarantee that those neighbors contain the correct answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On the other hand, an Inverted-File index reduces this work by organizing vectors into groups. During construction, clustering identifies representative centers and assigns vectors to nearby groups. A query can then select promising groups and search their contents. The parameter commonly called nprobe controls how many groups are examined. However, searching more groups generally improves recall but also increases work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Imagine one million passages divided into 1000 groups. Searching 10 groups might involve roughly 10K passages rather than the entire million. Of course, real groups are uneven, and selecting them also has a cost. The main tradeoff is that a useful passage can belong to a group that is skipped by the search. These groups are mathematical neighborhoods, not tidy subject folders. A travel-disruption rule might sit near insurance documents rather than ordinary expense policies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>IVF therefore introduces approximation. It saves work by accepting some risk of missing the nearest vectors.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Following Connections to the Right Neighborhood</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) avoids exhaustive comparisons by building routes between vectors. Its structure is a graph. In other words, points are connected by links.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each point represents a vector. The links provide routes through the collection. HNSW organizes these connections into layers, with sparse upper layers and a detailed bottom layer containing all vectors.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this approach, search starts near the top and moves toward points closer to the query. It then descends through the layers, progressively refining the search. At the bottom, it explores a broader set of nearby candidates to select the results.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You can think of this navigation like travelling through a road network. Major routes help reach the right area, while local roads help locate a specific destination. HNSW uses this broad-to-detailed pattern to avoid visiting every point.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Like the Inverted-File index, it performs approximate nearest-neighbor search. However, selected routes can miss a true nearest neighbor. Its benefit is that useful results can often be found with substantially fewer comparisons.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is no fixed collection size at which flat search must give way to Inverted-File or HNSW. Hardware, vector dimensions, query volume, memory, filtering, and latency requirements all influence the choice. HNSW is a strong candidate when memory permits, but we cannot say that it is automatically the best option for every workload.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A collection searched a few times per day creates a different problem from one serving thousands of simultaneous users. Vector count alone cannot capture that difference.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Much Searching Is Enough?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Approximate search creates a measurable tradeoff between speed and recall.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s say an exact search identifies the 10 nearest vectors. An approximate search returns eight of those same vectors and two others. This measures how closely the approximate search reproduces exact nearest-neighbor results. It doesn’t measure whether the returned passages really answer the employee’s question. Both index recall and actual evidence relevance need evaluation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>HNSW has several settings that have an impact on this tradeoff:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>M controls graph connectivity. Higher values generally provide more routes, improving recall while increasing memory use and construction work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>ef_construction controls how broadly the algorithm searches for suitable connections during insertion. A larger value generally produces a better graph but takes longer to build.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>ef_search controls the breadth of candidate exploration during a query. Increasing it generally improves recall while increasing search latency. It isn’t the number of results returned or a fixed count of visited points.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The application may need five passages while exploring a much larger candidate set to find them. Result count and search effort are separate decisions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For tuning, we should use representative questions and actual performance measurements. If a broader search consistently finds a previously missed cancellation exception, the added latency may be worthwhile. However, if answers don’t improve, changing the setting merely adds work.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The Closest Match Might Be the Wrong Policy</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Similarity must also be combined with rules about which documents are eligible.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, our employee needs the policy for their country and business unit, with an effective date that covers the journey. A highly similar passage from another region cannot help answer their query.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We use metadata filtering to define the eligible subset. The request becomes “find the most similar passages among current policies for this employee’s region.”</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Pre-filtering identifies eligible records before similarity ranking.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Post-filtering retrieves similarity candidates first and then removes records that fail the conditions.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If only two of the first 20 candidates qualify, post-filtering cannot supply 5 eligible results from that batch. Retrieving additional candidates may help, but requires more work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Nevertheless, pre-filtering is not automatically faster. The outcome depends on how selective the filter is and how the search engine combines filtering with its index. Graph search adds another complication. Disallowed points may still provide useful navigation routes toward allowed points. Blocking every such point during traversal can make eligible neighbors harder to reach.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Search engines can address this through filtering-aware graph structures, traversal strategies, or an exact scan when the eligible subset is small. Filtering can therefore be integrated into search rather than occurring entirely before or after it.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>What Happens When the Answer Changes?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The collection must remain correct as its documents change. For example, let’s say the company raises its hotel reimbursement limit from ₹5,000 to ₹7,000. If both versions remain eligible for current-policy searches, the assistant may retrieve either figure or receive contradictory evidence.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Changes to embedded text require new embeddings. However, an update doesn’t always require rebuilding every chunk. Unchanged chunks may be reusable, and stable identifiers can support replacing existing records.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A metadata-only change can often be applied without re-embedding, provided that metadata was not a part of the text used to create the vector. Some vector databases can expose separate operations for changing vectors and metadata.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For our policy example, a sensible design can prepare the new version’s chunks, verify their availability, and then change which version is eligible for current searches. Older versions can remain accessible for historical questions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That transition requires some sort of coordination. Deleting old chunks first can create a temporary gap. Inserting new chunks first can create temporary duplication. Version identifiers and explicit active-version rules help make the change predictable. Lastly, changing the embedding model requires similar planning but on a much larger scale. Existing documents generally need embeddings in the new model’s space, and queries must use the matching representation.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>From Promising Matches to a Supported Answer</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The final retrieval step turns promising matches into evidence the LLM can use. For example, a vector search might return 30 candidate passages. A reranker can compare each passage’s text with the question and select the most useful few.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/7249292e-5137-4dfd-b3af-39cbbbe2967f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/edeec364-514a-4cf8-87a6-06132f80c98b_3622x1310.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":527,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":198847,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/215151603?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fedeec364-514a-4cf8-87a6-06132f80c98b_3622x1310.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="199.0728021978022" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fVSY!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fedeec364-514a-4cf8-87a6-06132f80c98b_3622x1310.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Hybrid search adds another source of candidates by combining semantic retrieval with keyword-based retrieval. Embeddings help connect “cancelled flight” with “travel disruption,” while keyword search can preserve exact matches for policy identifiers, names, or unusual technical terms. Reranking can refine the combined results.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The application then supplies the selected text and source details to the LLM. For the stranded employee, this should include the current reimbursement rule, the relevant conditions, and enough context to explain how the policy applies to their situation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The search must also accommodate the scenario of an unanswered question. Every collection has nearest vectors, even when none might contain useful information. Returning the closest passage doesn’t mean that an answer exists. For example, if the retrieved documents discuss ordinary hotel bookings but say nothing about cancellations, the assistant should explain clearly that the available policy details don’t have a clear answer.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Finding a useful passage among thousands of documents requires several parts of an LLM application to work together. Documents first become smaller, meaningful chunks. Embeddings represent those chunks as vectors, allowing the search system to connect a question with passages that express related ideas, even when their wording differs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As the collection grows, indexes make that search more efficient. Flat search compares every eligible vector, while IVF and HNSW reduce the work through grouping or graph navigation. These approaches introduce tradeoffs between speed, memory, and recall that need to be measured against real questions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Similarity alone, however, cannot establish whether a passage is suitable evidence. Metadata filters help select the correct region, document type, or policy version. Careful updates keep outdated and duplicate passages from appearing in current searches. Hybrid search and reranking can further improve the evidence selected for the LLM.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>The final answer depends on the quality of this entire process. For the employee stranded at the airport, success means finding the current reimbursement rule, preserving its conditions, and explaining it clearly.</span></p></div></div><div underline;">Unsplash</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One morning, my pager went off at 2:14. (This was back when Amazon forced us to have physical pagers like the cool kids in the 90s.) It made a harsh and grating sound that I still remember to this day.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A service I owned had stopped accepting traffic. Three downstream teams were also paged. The service had shut down because a certificate had expired at midnight. Renewing it wasn’t difficult; it took about 20 minutes to complete.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What bothered me afterward wasn’t that we had missed it but, rather, </span><em><span>why</span></em><span> we had missed it. The team had spent the previous month in incident mode. Virtually every day there had been fires we had to put out.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Nobody was ignoring the certificate, or the dozen other small maintenance items like it. It was just that nobody had a free twenty minutes to remember those items existed. We were too busy fighting fires to do the work that prevented fires, and so the fires kept coming.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’ve seen this pattern everywhere. It shows up in software teams, in our careers, our households, and even our calendars. And once I first began to see it, I couldn’t help noticing it everywhere.</span></p><div class="subscribe-widget is-signed-up" data-component-name="SubscribeWidget" style="margin: 0 0 1em;direction: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You’ve probably seen the Eisenhower matrix. Everything you could do gets sorted along two axes, urgent or not, important or not, which gives you four boxes. The bottom row, the unimportant stuff, is easy. You either want to skip it or hand it off.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This article is about the top row, which describes the same work but at two different stages, because that’s where the trouble is.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And the trouble starts when we starve the first half of that top row.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Important and urgent” runs your day, because urgency is the absence of choice. When something is due at five, or a customer is waiting, or the service is down, you don’t decide whether to act. You just act.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Important but not urgent” has the opposite problem. Nothing in it has a deadline. Nothing in it has a person on the other end who will be disappointed if it doesn’t get done.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, you’ve been meaning to book a dentist appointment, but it keeps slipping. Now you need an emergency procedure.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Maybe you’ve been meaning to call an old friend, and every time you think of it, it’s too late in the evening, or you’re in the middle of something, and you’ll do it tomorrow. Eventually, an important relationship is lost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most explanations of the matrix leave out that the top two boxes are the same pile but at two different stages.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Everything important and urgent was, at some earlier point, important and not urgent. The expired certificate was once a mere maintenance task. But because it was deferred, it turned into a 2am page that woke up four teams.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The reason you’re buried in urgent work, and will stay buried, is that the important-but-not-urgent box, the half of the top row of the matrix, is being starved.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The cycle goes like this. Urgent things fill your plate. Non-urgent items get skipped. That skipped work turns urgent. Your urgent plate fills again, a little fuller than before. Repeat.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The end result? You’re always fighting fires.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You get stuck in this loop by being reasonable. Each time you handle only the thing that’s due today, you’ve made a sensible call. But that approach becomes a problem when that’s what every day turns into.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The only way out is to break the cycle. You have to find a way to do important things before they become urgent.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>What It Looks Like</span></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Starvation of important work, ironically, looks like a full calendar. Here’s what tends to get left out, and what it turns into.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Updating your resume while you like your job, instead of doing it in a panic after a re-org or layoff.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Writing down your accomplishments as they happen, instead of assembling them from memory a year later.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Telling your manager you want more scope, instead of finding out someone else got the project because they asked first.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Writing down how the system works while you still remember, instead of being the only person who can fix it, forever.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Fixing the process everyone works around, instead of waiting for it to break for real.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Going to the dentist regularly, instead of procrastinating until you need a root canal.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Prioritizing good sleep, instead of running on five hours and wondering why everything feels harder than it should.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Reaching out to a former colleague now, instead of when you need a favor.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Giving a peer feedback while the problem is small, instead of when it has become a problem with a name.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Checking in on your goals every quarter, instead of realizing in December that you forgot what they were.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Picking up the skill you’ll need in two years, instead of trying to learn it in the two weeks before you need it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Calling your parents, instead of wishing you had.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Writing your will or doing estate planning, instead of leaving it to someone else to decide what your wishes are.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Fixing the door that sticks, instead of shoving it for another five years.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>Breaking The Loop</span></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The cycle doesn’t break on its own. You have to break it on purpose.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Trace the fire back.</span></strong><span> After the next emergency, figure out what would have prevented it. Usually it’s something small and boring that never had a deadline. Then look at what’s sitting in your not-urgent-but-important pile right now. Does anything look like it might become urgent in the near future? If so, treat it as part of the cleanup. You’re already in firefighting mode, so extinguish the sparks that could cause the next potential fire while you’re there.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Make up a deadline.</span></strong><span> Important things often don’t come with a deadline, so give them one. This is how I finished my book. I had so many fires going that the only way it was going to happen was if I picked a date and treated it like it came from someone else. Parkinson’s law usually works against you: work expands to fill the time you give it. Give it less time, and it will shrink to fit.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Finish what you start.</span></strong><span> Here’s a pattern I see all the time. Things calm down for a week, you pick up something important, then halfway through, something urgent shows up, and you drop it. Now you’ve spent the time but gotten nothing. When you pick up a non-urgent thing, commit to finishing it. Extra hours spent on something that prevents the next fire is the best overtime you’ll ever work.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>An Exercise</span></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Think back to the last three emergencies you had to deal with at work or at home. Next to each one, write down the thing you could have done that would have prevented it or made it a much smaller incident.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now think about whether there’s something similar that you are putting off because there’s no urgency to it at the moment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s your next fire, but it hasn’t started yet. Pick a date, put it on the calendar, and finish it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Everything important is optional until it isn’t. Do it now while it’s still your choice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><strong>Enjoyed this week’s newsletter? Give it a ❤️ so I know to write similar ones in the future.</strong></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;hanging-punctuation: allow-end;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>A Life Engineered will always be a free publication, but if you’d like to support it, we’d be honored if you upgraded your subscription. Emoji', 'Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: 400;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>It’s rare to work with an unlimited token budget, but at OpenAI, that’s what all engineers, researchers, finance colleagues, and marketing folks do. Recently, I visited one of the world’s leading frontier labs to find out how OpenAI operates today – and for a glimpse at where software engineering might be headed as a profession.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Plenty has changed since I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aed2f1e3-dce2-4bc6-a03b-da581b34f402?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>visited</span></a><span> OpenAI’s headquarters last year. Within a year, Codex has gone from a “nice-to-have” tool to being the backbone of pretty much everything at the company.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To learn more, I talked with seven engineering leaders and engineers there: Venkat Venkataramani (VP of Engineering, Applied Infra), Sulman Choudhry (Head of Engineering, ChatGPT), Andrew Ambrosino (Lead, Desktop), Joe Gershenson (Lead, Core Agent team), Akshay Nathan (Engineering Lead, Productivity), Ahmed Ibrahim (Engineer, Codex) and Steve Coffey (Engineer, Responses API). </span><em><span>Thanks to all for taking part!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, we cover:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Codex takes over at OpenAI. </span></strong><span>In a matter of months, nearly all OpenAI’s non-engineers moved over to Codex and ChatGPT Work without a mandate from above for it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Death of the IDE & pull requests. </span></strong><span>IDE usage has been down since January when Codex usage started to surge. PRs and code reviews need to be rethought.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>OpenAI’s agentic software factory. </span></strong><span>OpenAI has built a “software factory” with several automated, agentic feedback loops: for example, Perf Factory monitors production and kicks off Codex agents to automatically fix performance issues.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>How engineering tooling & practices are changing. </span></strong><span>Hand-built internal tools are slowly being replaced by Codex, which is increasingly preferred for debugging over specialized tools. Harness efficiency is critical in software factories.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Engineering for a billion users: how OpenAI scales up its infra. </span></strong><span>They buy first and take it in-house later. Also, geographic infra distribution, capacity planning tactics and challenges.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Making OpenAI’s API more reliable and performant</span></strong><span>. CPUs are becoming a bottleneck, doing slower deployments on purpose, and solving load challenges.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>How the software engineering job is changing. </span></strong><span>Engineering specializations are disappearing, judgment and agency are more important, and it only takes one or two engineers for previously “impossible” rewrites and migrations to succeed.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Before we start, a scheduling update: I’m in New York for the week, attending the LDX3 conference and visiting a few startups and tech companies in the city,  so there will be no edition of The Pulse on Thursday. Normal service resumes next week!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>The bottom of this article could be cut off in some
