UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Solving load challenges</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, how does OpenAI respond to these challenges? Steve revealed the three biggest projects the team is taking on, currently:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Migrate from Python to Rust to reduce CPU load: </span></strong><span>the API layer was originally written in Python because researchers already use Python, so it’s much faster to iterate with a shared programming language.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The work the API does is input/output bound, so Python’s single-threaded processing should not be a problem assuming Python is optimized, which it was. But then, the workloads changed from being prompts: contexts increased, validation was added, safety logic was added, and more. Python’s performance downsides added up, so the API team has started a Rust rewrite.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A mere two engineers are working on this Python-to-Rust migration, and are making very heavy use of Codex. So far, they’ve rewritten 300,000 lines of code to Rust with no disruption to the service. Astra has been a major accelerator of the rewrite’s pace. Engineers told me they see a 3x increase in lines migrated between July and August using GPT-5.6, and also in the period August to September using Astra. Around 90% of Codex’s traffic is served through the Rust path and the team estimates the full migration will be complete in a few months.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Note from Gergely: it’s interesting to note that Anthropic came to the exact same conclusion, independently: their platform team is also </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/74bcc1d3-7654-4114-8c77-6a208ab08fb2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>busy migrating its API from Python to Rust.</span></a></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Tokenize only the deltas with WebSockets. </span></strong><span>The problem that agentic tool calling introduced was that the full context kept being re-tokenized at the API level, meaning that after each tool call which Codex made, the complete history had to be re-tokenized. For a tool chain with 40 tool calls, this meant re-tokenizing the growing context window 40 times, which means more CPU usage and greater latency. It also results in a quadratic latency degradation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Instead, with WebSocket streaming the API now tokenizes the context window once, then it stores the tokenized values in-memory, and tokenizes just the </span><em><span>delta</span></em><span> that comes back from the tool calls. By making this change, the API saw median request latency drop 30% practically overnight. As a bonus, CPU usage also fell.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Proactive capacity management for GPUs. </span></strong><span>While CPU usage has become challenging, there’s also a problem with GPUs: it takes 15-20 minutes to add GPU capacity from when demand arises because GPUs are not stateless. For them to function, the model needs to be loaded onto them, and OpenAI’s models are so large that it takes that long to copy over the weights and initialize the model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The OpenAI team is responding with capacity forecasting and “warming up” GPUs in advance: they load models onto GPUs in advance of demand. This type of capacity management has some similarities with spinning up a new machine – although adding a new pod to Kubernetes doesn’t involve 15 minutes of latency!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>7. How the software engineering job is changing</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I asked all seven people whom I talked to at OpenAI how the software engineering role is changing there in context of everything covered in this article. Some main themes emerged:</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Engineering specializations are disappearing</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are no more dedicated frontend or backend engineering roles, nor mobile engineer specialization. Sulman Choudhry, ChatGPT’s Head of Engineering, told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Although I always thought specialization in engineering would, one day, go away, it’s still surprising how quickly it has happened. Last year, teams were still looking for an Android or iOS engineer for specialized work. But no more. Today, if something needs to get done, you just need a builder.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Codex allows any builder to think at the problem’s own abstraction level. If, as an engineer, I understand user problems and have an intuition of how to solve them, I can do it, regardless of specialization.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Infra teams no longer receive questions on the support channel</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s interesting that while infra teams still have Slack channels for internal support, those channels are virtually silent because practically no one uses them for support. Instead, engineers just ask Codex how to do something and it looks up the documentation and builds it!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A by-product of this is that infra engineers have more bandwidth for other things and have taken on the work that infra product managers used to do: they now decide on priorities, scope work, and build it. On the infra team, every engineer is a sort of product manager / engineer hybrid.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>What matters to engineers</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I asked VP of Engineering, Applied Infra, Venkat Venkataramani, and also the Head of Engineering ChatGPT, Sulman Choudhry, what sets the best engineers apart:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Judgment</span></strong><span>: is an approach the right one, or is another more optimal? Should a feature be shipped or binned?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Prioritization: </span></strong><span>what’s the next most important thing to work on and what is not worth doing, right now?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Agency</span></strong><span>: the best engineers relentlessly come up with ideas and parallelize with agents as much as possible without being prompted.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Taste</span></strong><span>: what does “great” actually look like? Engineers with good taste produce standout artifacts in functionality, architecture, design, etc.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>New engineering layer at the AI-agent level</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A lot more engineering effort at OpenAI goes towards solving the problem of how to make the agent / agent loop more effective. solution for this?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How do I iterate on the solution?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How do I share my artifact generated with people and get feedback?</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The big difference I see is that non-developers are realizing they can build software solutions for their problems.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span> Just one or two people can make “impossible” rewrites & migrations succeed</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Prior to Codex, the Python-to-Rust API migration mentioned above would have probably been a six-person job of slow progress. Today, this has transformed to only needing two people who make rapid progress and get it done in just a few months. Rewrites and migrations that would have needed large teams before now involve just a couple of engineers and lots of Codex agents. </span><em><span>This is not too dissimilar to how migrations and rewrites are done at Anthropic, like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c86113ce-3761-400a-9906-515b1b537e58?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>the Bun migration.</span></a></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Takeaways</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Thanks again to everyone at OpenAI who contributed to this article. </span></em><span>The pace of change there since the last time I visited surprised me, especially how rapidly Codex/ChatGPT Work has spread among non-engineers, who are now using AI to create “artifacts” like documents, spreadsheets, slides and websites.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>It’s OpenAI’s “agentic software factory” that I find most impressive. </span></strong><span>It’s now possible to build agentic systems that act on CI errors and warnings to produce fixes and then re-run CI, and also take action on code review comments. Since AI agents can also do code review comments, they can iterate on pull requests and fix obvious issues before a human gets involved. OpenAI also has a “Perf Factory” service that monitors production and raises fixes to further improve the system!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These capabilities are new and clearly useful. I’ve seen glimpses of similar, less ambitious proto-software factories elsewhere, in the form of agents one-shotting bug fixes based on customer reports, and submitting them for review. But OpenAI’s setup is by far the most advanced.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Agents “babysitting” deploys feels like a novel and useful deployment strategy. </span></strong><span>Rolling out changes to large systems used to be done in responsible fashion via gradual rollouts by engineers. It’s notable that OpenAI has managed to build a system that is able to do this rollout autonomously, with an agent taking ownership of the rollout.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Of course, it can’t be forgotten that at OpenAI, token budgets do not exist and that the company is in the business of selling tokens. </span></strong><span>If asked, I would caution against blindly copying innovations there for no other reason than the potential cost! But at OpenAI, they’re sparing no expense to build ever more capable AI models, and so far, the strategy is paying off handsomely.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Considering how the price of tokens is falling for models that are </span><em><span>almost</span></em><span> as good as the very best ones, it’s possible to predict that per-token costs will continue to drop. If so, more companies will be able to afford to not worry so much about the cost of tokens, and to set up similar agentic loops like what OpenAI already has in place.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>One thing looks certain: cutting-edge and “AI-native” companies are likely to build software in ways that are much closer to what OpenAI does today than to the more traditional software development lifecycle of the 2010s and early 2020s.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;hanging-punctuation: allow-end;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxNTgxMjI5MywicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3ODk0ODczMDUsImV4cCI6MjEwNTA2MzMwNSwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.sWufRI8lb2qN5_sLWBnhyD9XfCFXhZKhosAbNJnDhfc?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. This email is intended for a single recipient, but occasional forwarding is totally fine.</em></p><p class="button-wrapper" rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An LLM can analyze a 100-page document, follow a complicated programming discussion, and refer back to something discussed several messages ago. However, as soon as we open a new chat where the earlier conversation is not present, it immediately forgets everything. It appears that LLMs have the memory of a goldfish.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This observation is indeed true. LLMs usually have no personal or persistent memory of previous interactions. So, how is it able to refer to what we’ve said in the past?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In truth, an LLM doesn’t remember a conversation like human beings do. However, it receives information about the conversation so far with each new message that we send to the LLM. All of this is handled by the application that is built around the model and not by the model itself. For example, a chat application might store messages, maintain summaries of earlier discussions, retrieve relevant memories, and maintain a user profile. It can then place some of that information in front of the model as needed. From the user’s perspective, the model appears to remember. But technically, the surrounding application is doing most of the remembering.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This difference between the model and the application around the model is the key to understanding LLM memory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This design has important consequences. As a conversation grows, the application must keep processing more text, thereby increasing cost and latency. Eventually, the conversation ends up turning too large to fit inside the model’s context window. At that point, older information must be removed, summarized, or stored somewhere else.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we will learn how LLMs handle memory so that they are useful to end users in performing complex tasks that require conversation and holding context.</span></p><div 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the context of LLMs, the word “memory” is used for several different things that should not be confused. Let’s look at each type in detail.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Trained Memory</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>During training, an LLM learns patterns from enormous amounts of data. These patterns are encoded in billions of numerical values called parameters or weights.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is why a model can explain JavaScript, recognize a common historical event, or write an email without receiving that knowledge in the current prompt.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But this is not personal memory. If a user tells the model, “My preferred programming language is TypeScript,” a normal API response does not rewrite the model’s weights. The base model does not permanently learn that fact from the conversation.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Working Memory</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The model’s temporary working memory is its context window. This contains everything the model can consider while generating its current response.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>{</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “messages”: [</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    {</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “role”: “user”,</span></span>

<span class="line"><span>  “messages”: [</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    {</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “role”: “user”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “content”: “What is my name?”</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    }</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  ]</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>}</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The model can’t reliably answer because the second request doesn’t include the name. The earlier request has already finished. And there is no private diary that exists inside the model that is kept updated.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For the conversation to work, the application must send the earlier exchange again:</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>{</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “messages”: [</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    {</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “role”: “user”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “content”: “My name is Adam.”</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    },</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    {</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “role”: “assistant”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “content”: “Nice to meet you, Adam.”</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    },</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    {</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “role”: “user”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “content”: “What is my name?”</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    }</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  ]</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>}</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now the model answers “Adam” because the name is visible in the current input.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most model providers have a stateless Messages API that requires the conversation history to be supplied for a multi-turn conversation.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Does Every API Call Really Start From Zero?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A new model invocation doesn’t typically start without any knowledge. The model still has several things:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Its trained weights</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Its general language abilities</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Knowledge acquired during training</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Safety and behavioral instructions supplied by the platform</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Everything included in the current context</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What it lacks is an automatically updated memory of this particular user or conversation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A better way to put it is that every response is generated from the model’s existing weights plus the context made available for that response. Information from the conversation history is not available unless the surrounding system carries it forward.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some APIs offer server-managed conversation state. In such a case, we don’t need to resend every message manually. We can provide a conversation identifier, and the server locates the previous messages based on that identifier to reconstruct the necessary context. This makes the API easier to use, but it doesn’t mean that the model has developed a personal memory.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How AI Chatbots Create the Illusion of Memory</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Suppose a conversation contains five user messages and five assistant responses.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When the user sends the next message, the application may construct an input that contains the following details:</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>System instructions</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>User message 1</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Assistant response 1</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>User message 2</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Assistant response 2</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>User message 3</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Assistant response 3</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>User message 4</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Assistant response 4</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>User message 5</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Assistant response 5</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>New user message</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The model receives all of this as one large input. For example, in the earlier conversation, the user may have mentioned a database problem, selected PostgreSQL, and asked for TypeScript examples. Therefore, it can continue the answers based on this path in a more natural manner.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To the user, this might feel like the model has remembered things from earlier. However, from the perspective of the model, those details are simply present in the text that is being processed right now. We can’t simply call it “fake memory” because there is real continuity at the application level. A better term for this is reconstructed memory or context-based memory.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The Context Window is a Working-Memory Budget</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A context window of an LLM is measured in tokens. Tokens are small pieces of text. A short word may be one token, while a longer or unusual word may be split into several tokens.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The context window normally contains more than the visible conversation. It may also contain hidden instructions, tool definitions, search results, documents, and space for the answer. Imagine a hypothetical model with a 100K-token context window. An application might need to fit the following into that space:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>System instructions: 3,000 tokens</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Tool definitions: 8,000 tokens</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Conversation history: 55,000 tokens</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Retrieved documents: 20,000 tokens</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Current question: 1,000 tokens</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Remaining response budget: 13,000 tokens</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Once the available space is exhausted, the application can’t just keep adding information indefinitely. It must remove, compress, or replace something.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A large context window also doesn’t guarantee perfect recall. As the amount of information grows, it can become harder for the model to differentiate important facts from irrelevant, repetitive, or contradictory material. This degradation is also known as “context rot”. We need to select useful context even if we have a very large context window at our disposal. Therefore, the context window is both a capacity limit and an attention-management problem.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Why Long Conversations Become Expensive</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LLM APIs commonly charge for the number of input and output tokens processed. Let’s say each completed conversational round adds approximately 1000 tokens.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Request 1 processes approximately 1,000 tokens.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Request 2 processes approximately 2,000 tokens.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Request 3 processes approximately 3,000 tokens.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Request 10 processes approximately 10,000 tokens.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Across those ten requests, the application has processed approximately 55K tokens of input.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The visible conversation contains only about 10,000 tokens, but earlier parts have been processed repeatedly. A long system prompt, large tool definitions, and retrieved documents can increase this cost even further.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Longer contexts also increase latency. This is because more information needs to be processed before the model starts to answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Techniques like prompt caching can help alleviate costs, but they don’t create memory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Providers can cache a repeated prefix such as the system prompt and previous conversation history. When the next request begins with the same content, the provider may reuse previously computed information. This can reduce cost and latency. However, cached tokens consume part of the context window. Caching merely changes how efficiently repeated context is processed. It doesn’t give the model unlimited memory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Prompt caching is therefore an optimization, not a memory architecture.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>What Happens When the Context Window Fills Up?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is no single universal behavior that LLMs perform when the context window fills up. Depending on the API and application, several things may happen.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The API may reject the request because it is too large.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The application may remove the oldest messages.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A chat product may manage history using a rolling window.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The system may replace old material with a compact summary.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Some APIs also provide server-side compaction mechanisms.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Compaction is carrying forward important state in a smaller representation so that long-running interactions continue with lower context usage. This means a very long chat may not contain every original sentence in its active context. The model may instead receive something like:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Conversation summary:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The user is building an invoice service in TypeScript.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>PostgreSQL was selected as the database.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The API uses Express and Prisma.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The current problem concerns duplicate invoice creation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Previous attempts involving application-level checks failed under concurrency.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The summary preserves the central state while discarding greetings, repeated explanations, abandoned ideas, and low-value details. The tradeoff is that summarization is lossy. A small detail that seemed unimportant during summarization may become important later.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The Main Techniques to Extend Memory</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Real applications usually combine several techniques to extend memory instead of relying on one. Let’s look at a few techniques in detail.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Sliding-window Memory</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A sliding window keeps only the most recent portion of the conversation. When new messages arrive, the oldest ones are removed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, the application might always retain:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An embedding is a numerical representation of meaning. This means that texts concerning similar ideas receive similar representations even when they don’t use exactly the same words.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, let’s say the user asks: “Why did we reject Redis for the invoice service?” The memory system searches for past passages semantically related to “Redis,” “invoice service”, and “rejected architecture decisions.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It may retrieve information such as “we decided against Redis because the deployment environment does not provide a managed Redis service, and PostgreSQL advisory locks already cover the required coordination.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Only the retrieved passage is added to the current context. Here’s how the process works roughly:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Store selected pieces of earlier conversations.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Convert those pieces into embeddings.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Convert the new question into an embedding.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Find semantically similar memories.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Filter and rank the candidates.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Insert the best candidates into the model’s prompt.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This doesn’t enlarge the context window. It selects which memories deserve space inside it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, vector retrieval can also sometimes fail. It may retrieve something similar but irrelevant. It can miss a memory because it was phrased strangely. It can also come up with an outdated decision. Metadata such as user ID, project ID, date, and memory type is therefore essential to make sense of this data.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Long-term User Profiles</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A long-term profile stores durable facts that may be useful across many conversations. For example, this could include things like:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The user generally prefers beginner-friendly technical explanations.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Examples should use TypeScript where practical.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Explanations should use complete paragraphs rather than fragmented bullets.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A profile should contain stable preferences, not every passing statement. For example, “I am testing Python today” is probably session information. On the other hand, “I use Python for all data projects” may be a durable preference if repeatedly confirmed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We also need to update profiles. This is because preferences can change over time. Good systems attach timestamps, sources, and sometimes confidence scores to memory entries.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Cross-session Memory Works</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cross-session memory means that information survives after one chat ends and can influence another chat.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A typical implementation works like this:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>During or after a conversation, a memory process identifies potentially durable information.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It stores that information in a user-level, project-level, or organization-level memory store.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A future conversation starts.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The application selects memories relevant to the new conversation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Those memories are inserted into the new conversation’s context.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The model generates its response using the supplied memories.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" is number five. The new model call still needs the remembered information placed into its current context.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we’ve looked at LLM memory in detail. The key takeaways are as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Model weights contain general knowledge learned during training.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The context window contains information available for the current response.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Conversation storage holds previous messages.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Long-term memory stores selected facts, preferences, and past events.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The memory manager decides what to retrieve and place on the desk.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It can be said that LLMs, along with the application surrounding them, don’t have the memory of a goldfish. They can process an enormous amount of information at once. But they don’t automatically carry personal experiences from one call to the next.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>What appears to be memory is a carefully constructed system of context reconstruction, summarization, retrieval, and persistent storage. The quality of an LLM application’s memory depends at least as much on the surrounding architecture as it does on the model itself.</span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" item.title: The Executive Loop
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Executive Loop

Jade Rubick

The job of an executive follows a very simple algorithm: (1) Figure out what needs to happen. (2) Figure out how to make it happen. (3) Make it happen. This is simple, but it’s not easy. In fact, it’s so simple it seems dumb to lay it out. But it’s surprisingly... well, not something people take to automatically.

#Leadership Management
item.description: The Executive Loop

item.title: Confessions Of An Unrepentant Slop Snob
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Confessions Of An Unrepentant Slop Snob

Charity Majors

“So maybe we all just need to be ruthlessly outcome-oriented. Build the best thing we can, as fast as we can. AI is a powerful and versatile tool, so we should use it wherever we can to make our work better and do it faster. Is it really that simple? I had nearly convinced myself that it was, when I noticed how contradictory my own behavior had become.” Charity shares a framework for thinking about when AI involvement is additive or a violation.

#Management CareerGrowth AI
item.description: Confessions Of An Unrepentant Slop Snob

item.title: Why I Stopped Arguing With People
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Why I Stopped Arguing With People

Cong Wang

“Over the years I’ve slowly stopped arguing. Not because I stopped caring about being right, but because I finally understood what an argument actually is, and what it can and cannot do. Here is what changed my mind.”

#Communication Influence
item.description: Why I Stopped Arguing With People

item.title: We Are All Product Engineers Now
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
We Are All Product Engineers Now

Laurie Voss

“This post is an attempt to build on those and make a forecast of where the industry is going in the next 10 years. Making a 10 year forecast of anything is of course a crazy thing to try to do, and especially about the business of software right now. To make it, I had to make two very big assumptions.”

#AI Product IndustryTrends
item.description: We Are All Product Engineers Now

item.title: What Is Happening With Code Reviews?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
What Is Happening With Code Reviews?

Gergely Orosz

“One question haunting the minds of CTOs and heads of engineering whom I’ve been talking with, is how to deal with large quantities of code review which have only been growing now that AI agents generate most code at many tech companies.”

#Management AI CodeReview
item.description: What Is Happening With Code Reviews?

item.title: How Well Do Agents Use Test And Verification Techniques?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How Well Do Agents Use Test And Verification Techniques?

Dan Luu

“Here, we test if simple instructions to agents to use particular techniques or libraries improve implementation correctness, as a kind of test to see how effective agents are when guided by someone with no expertise in testing who's maybe heard that you should apply certain techniques or use certain libraries.”

#AI Testing Agents
item.description: How Well Do Agents Use Test And Verification Techniques?

item.title: The Startup's Postgres Survival Guide
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Startup's Postgres Survival Guide

Alexander Belanger

“Over the past half year or so, I’ve been writing an internal doc for our engineers trying to distill two years of Postgres battles into a somewhat cohesive document. While I love the Postgres manual, I find it’s hard to turn to when shit hits the fan because it’s just so darn comprehensive. I thought this might be useful for others and would appreciate feedback (or other tidbits that you’ve learned running Postgres in production).”

#Guide Database PostgreSQL
item.description: The Startup's Postgres Survival Guide

However, when we ask the same question twice to an LLM, it will most likely produce two differently worded answers. Both of those answers may be acceptable. But it makes evaluation tricky. To evaluate an LLM, we have to measure whether the application continues to behave properly across many situations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“LLM-as-a-Judge” is one part of this evaluation process. A healthy LLM evaluation system combines several ingredients such as conventional software tests, carefully curated examples, automated checks, model-based judging, human review, and production monitoring.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we are going to look at the process of LLM evaluation in detail. 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>What Does it Mean for an LLM Application to be Healthy?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When can we call an LLM healthy?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The answer is quite simple. An LLM is deemed healthy if it consistently generates useful results while remaining within acceptable limits for accuracy, safety, speed, reliability, and cost. For example, consider a customer-support assistant. We cannot say it is healthy by a single question such as “Did it return the correct output?”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We need to consider several different questions:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did it understand what the customer was asking?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Was the answer factually correct based on the company documentation?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did it answer the entire question?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did it follow the required tone and format?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did it avoid inventing policies that do not exist?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did it refuse requests that it should not answer?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did it respond within an acceptable amount of time?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did the request cost an acceptable amount to process?</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As we can see, these questions are all related to different dimensions of quality, where each dimension is important. We can have an assistant that is friendly and relevant, but it might generate factually incorrect answers. It might be accurate but so verbose that users can’t simply find the answer. It might produce excellent answers but take 30 seconds for every request. Therefore, while evaluating an LLM, we must measure multiple aspects of the system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We also need to differentiate between the health of the LLM and the application. We can’t simply label the model as the source of all problems. The problems can be caused by various sources. For example, we might have an incorrect prompt, missing documents, poor retrieval logic, incorrect tool calls, stale data, or a change in the surrounding code.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Why Ordinary Tests Are Not Sufficient for LLMs?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Traditional software tests usually depend on deterministic behavior. If a function receives a known input, the test expects a specific output. For example:</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>Input: add(2, 3)</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Expected output: 5</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This type of test works only because there is one exact correct answer. However, an LLM’s task is different. For example, consider the question “Explain why a password reset link may expire”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One possible response might begin by talking about security. Another response might first explain the expiration period. The way the sentences are written may be totally different even though the underlying answers are correct.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/2a120a73-b629-4fa5-87a0-9d7179a929f8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Three properties make LLM evaluation tricky.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First, the outputs from an LLM are not deterministic. This is because LLMs generate answers using a probability-based approach. We can use the same prompt and model, but the answers may be different. Increasing the model’s temperature only increases the variation. But even if we set a low temperature, it doesn’t make every model and infra combination perfectly repeatable.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even an exact string comparison can mark many valid answers as failures. For example, the sentences “The payment was declined because the card expired” and “The card’s expiration date caused the payment to fail” convey the same information.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Second, quality is multidimensional and partly subjective. We can’t have a universally correct level of detail, tone, or organization of the answer. A response appropriate for a developer may simply confuse the customer. A short answer may work well in a support chat. But a longer answer might be more suitable in documentation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This doesn’t imply that quality is impossible to measure. It just means that we need to first define the desired qualities. For example, having a goal like “give a good answer” is too vague to test. A much better option could be something like “Answer the question directly, use only the supplied policy, and explain all required steps”.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Third, the correctness also depends on the context. For example, the answer to “Can this order be refunded?” depends on multiple data points such as order date, product type, account status, region, and current refund policy. A particular response might be correct for one customer and wrong for another.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To evaluate properly, we must therefore include the context available to the model. We must be able to test whether the answer is correct relative to that context.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, traditional testing is still needed for the deterministic parts of an LLM application. For example, things like JSON parsing, permission checks, calculations, database operations, API contracts, and tool execution should continue to rely on the usual unit and integration tests.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The Basic Evaluation Loop</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A practical LLM evaluation system is built around a repeated process that works as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Collect representative test cases.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Run the application on those cases.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Inspect the resulting answers with several evaluation methods.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Compare the results with the current production version.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Block or investigate changes that cause an important regression.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Monitor real production traffic for problems that the test set missed.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Add newly discovered failures back into the test set.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 super important. We need to evolve the useful evaluation dataset by adding more examples. Such a dataset grows as real users reveal unexpected questions, ambiguous instructions, document formats, and new ways the system can fail.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Golden Datasets for Repeatable Tests for LLM Behavior</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A golden dataset is a carefully curated collection of possible inputs and information about what a good response to such an input should contain. Think of it as something that plays a role similar to a unit-testing suite. But unlike unit tests, we don’t always check the answers based on exact equality.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, a test case for a refund assistant might contain the following details:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0
