discussion, Ben also gave a clear preference on deployment posture. He said he would avoid active-standby as much as possible and run something like this as active as possible, since active-standby earns its place mainly when you have state to manage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The lesson even applies beyond payments. Some chokepoints are part of the structure, because the architecture needs one place where cross-boundary decisions happen. The best way to deal with that is to make that chokepoint simple enough to trust, and spend the engineering budget on keeping it that way.</span></p><h1 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(2em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Credit Card Authorization Flow</span></h1><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us now look at a card authorization flow that we got from the American Express team to understand how things work even more clearly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The journey of a transaction starts outside the American Express systems. A card gets used at a merchant’s point-of-sale terminal. From there, the sequence goes as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The Global Transaction Router receives the request first.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The router applies deterministic or priority-based routing. The choice depends on the use case.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Inside the cell, a collection of microservices performs validation, enrichment, transformation, and issuer determination.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The cell returns the transaction to the router.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The router sends the request to the appropriate card issuers for authorization.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The issuer response arrives back at the router.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The router uses deterministic routing to reach the cell holding the context of the transaction for authorization.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The cell validates the response.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The transaction travels back to the merchant’s acquiring bank.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The final confirmation of the payment is sent back to the POS terminal.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One thing to note is that the cell never contacts the card issuer directly. This preserves the rule that cells should not communicate with anything beyond their boundaries.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below that shows the process in detail:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(2em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Mid-Transaction Failure</span></h1><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us now return to the transaction that we talked about at the beginning of the article.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Payments processing at American Express uses an orchestrated microservices architecture. This means one orchestrator microservice manages the workflow and calls the other microservices in turn. This orchestrator also monitors the health of those microservices continuously and detects failures.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here is the full sequence of events that happen once a required service starts failing, or when too few instances of that service are running to handle it.:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The orchestrator detects the failure and halts processing.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It sends the transaction back to the Global Transaction Router.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The router selects a healthy cell.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Processing restarts in that cell using the original transaction data.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The last step is where the design diverges. American Express discards the partial work. Every microservice call the failing cell completed gets thrown away, and the second cell starts from the beginning with the same input. This rerouting covers both new transactions arriving at the failing cell and transactions already in flight inside it.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/976c93ce-6f7b-4fe0-a8d6-30e7ab604734?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The reasoning behind this approach goes back to the boundary problem. Resuming a transaction would require the second cell to read state from the first. However, that link would create shared state between cells. Shared state brings synchronization problems and consistency risks during failover, which is the exact problem this architecture seeks to avoid.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The result of this choice is that cells stay loosely coupled. Each cell runs its own database clusters, the microservices inside a cell communicate with the local cluster only, and a rerouted transaction is processed with zero reliance on state from the previous cell. The orchestrator also runs application health checks against the service mesh’s readiness endpoints. When overall cell health degrades past an acceptable threshold, the orchestrator reports the cell as unavailable.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Redoing completed work sounds wasteful. However, the trade-off works because a payment is short, so redoing a few hundred milliseconds costs very little against the alternative of a permanent structural dependency between every pair of cells. In a system where one unit of work runs for minutes, checkpointing might seem more favorable as an approach.</span></p><h1 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(2em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Recovery Semantics</span></h1><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Restarting a transaction elsewhere can be done up to a specific moment. Think of it like a point of no return. The exact position of that moment is a design decision that a team needs to make.  For example, rerouting is safe while a transaction remains inside the core payments ecosystem, and once it has gone to an external system such as a card issuer, it stays where it is.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Card authorizations are structured so the point of no return falls toward the end of processing. American Express placed the irreversible step as late as the payment flow allows, making the recoverable window as wide as it can be.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" where late rerouting of the transaction is not possible, safety comes from idempotency.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each transaction carries a unique identifier consistent across every retry and reroute, and downstream systems use it to suppress duplicates. Failback is controlled with canary capabilities using percentages. They avoid bouncing everything back the moment a cell returns. Also, shifting traffic by percentage lets American Express drain a cell gradually, validate a recovering cell under partial load, or respond carefully during an incident.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But this opens up another question: How does the platform prevent a recovered cell from writing stale state after its transactions moved elsewhere?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are three mechanisms here that narrow the window:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Speed:</span></strong><span> Card payments move so fast that by the time a failed cell returns, the transaction has usually completed elsewhere.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Idempotency identifiers:</span></strong><span> Duplicate suppression happens downstream, using the identifier that travelled with the transaction.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Paced recovery:</span></strong><span> Percentage-based traffic control governs when and how much work a recovering cell receives.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The specific details can vary. Recovery in finance might mean waiting for something to sync, accepting eventual consistency, or creating a compensating transaction, depending on the transaction type and where the failure occurred.</span></p><h1 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(2em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Design Tradeoffs</span></h1><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us now look at the trade-offs in the architecture implemented by American Express.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Duplicated services:</span></strong><span> Enforcing the boundary sometimes produces duplicate implementations of the same service across cells. American Express accepts this cost because it preserves cell independence and removes cross-cell network hops. Naturally, preventing cross-cell dependencies grows harder as a platform grows, so the cost increases over time.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Dropped log records:</span></strong><span> The buffer truncation policy means that under sustained pressure, the platform keeps processing transactions while losing part of the record of what it did. To be clear, these are application logs meant for general observability and not critical transactional events.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Delayed global visibility: </span></strong><span>Each cell writes logs, metrics, and traces locally first, with aggregation to global dashboards happening asynchronously. Losing part of the stack degrades visibility for one cell instead of the platform. The global view always lags.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Rejected transactions: </span></strong><span>Data synchronization between cells runs asynchronously. The consistency requirements depend on the transaction type and the business rule. When a transaction requires strong consistency, but the required data cannot be validated or turns out to be inconsistent, American Express may reject that transaction to preserve data integrity.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also, one thing to note about cells is that they change how many fail at once rather than how often failures happen, since running more independent units arguably produces more individual failures. In other words, management overhead and complexity are traded off for reduced impact of a failure.</span></p><h1 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(2em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Conclusion</span></h1><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The payment platform built by the American Express engineering team survives a cell failure because the design doesn’t allow one transaction to depend on two cells at once.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here are the key points that make it work:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Two data strategies, one goal:</span></strong><span> Reference data that changes rarely gets pushed to every cell ahead of time, while data that changes constantly stays put and the transaction travels to it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>A thin component at the chokepoint:</span></strong><span> The Global Transaction Router carries enormous responsibility and very little logic, which makes it dependable.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Restart in place of resume:</span></strong><span> Discarding partial work costs a few hundred milliseconds and removes the shared state that would link every cell to every other cell.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>A recovery window with a chosen position: </span></strong><span>Placing the point of no return late in the sequence widens the range in which failure remains survivable.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Recovery semantics from the domain:</span></strong><span> The pattern provides structure, and business logic provides the rules for what a partially completed transaction requires.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px Symbol';font-weight: 400;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>One question haunting the minds of CTOs and heads of engineering whom I’ve been talking with, is how to deal with large quantities of code review which have only been growing now that AI agents generate most code at many tech companies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since the end of 2025, it has seemed that the era of devs writing code by hand </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3870c4ce-a7ce-4273-9811-d9c8e63ba35d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>is over</span></a><span> at startups and in Big Tech. AI agents work faster and generate more pull requests (PRs) than devs ever did, and the size of those pull requests is also increasing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today’s article summarizes some approaches to code review at various workplaces in this new paradigm, covering:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Humans review the AI code reviews. </span></strong><span>The most popular approach: AI code review tools go through code changes, and devs review the review itself.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Triage by “blast radius” & decide an approach. </span></strong><span>Low-risk changes don’t need human review, and high-risk ones do. Adopted by OpenAI, Anthropic, and others.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Review the plan/tests/database schema, but not implementation. </span></strong><span>Focus on reviewing the “before” and “after” states of an implementation, rather than the implementation itself.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Produce less code. </span></strong><span>Set up AI agents to produce smaller PRs that are easier to review and reason about.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Review everything by hand. </span></strong><span>Not everyone has adopted AI code review tools – even those that have sometimes still expect devs to read through all the new code, before allowing it to go to prod.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>No human code review? </span></strong><span>There’s more talk about dropping human code reviews than there is evidence of this actually happening, so far. The most I could find was AI startups doing it and building additional layers for safer production rollouts.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Why do we review code, anyway? </span></strong><span>Before figuring out whether or not code review should stay, it’s worth going back to the fundamental technical, team, and organizational reasons for code reviews.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Unsurprisingly, it’s clear there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to the question of how to handle a deluge of AI-generated code review. </span><em><span>Please leave a comment below about how your team or company deals with this new, pressing issue!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A snapshot of what’s going on in code review at this stage of AI development is provided by the graphic from GitHub, below. The background context it provides is pretty stark. It shows the stats for the number of PRs and commits over the course of three years on the popular platform:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: To find out more, I asked around.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>1. Humans review the AI code reviews</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The most common approach is to add an AI code review step to every pull request in a variety of ways:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Use one or more vendors to review PRs. </span></strong><span>There are dozens of vendors offering this functionality – ones like CodeRabbit, Gitar, Greptile, GitHub Copilot Code Review, Qodo, Claude Code Review, Ellipsis and more. Many teams choose one or more, and the bots then review PRs, leaving comments for devs. For example, the Bun project by Anthropic has CodeRabbit, GitHub Code Review, and Claude Code Review </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c81dc28e-0517-4335-a143-14fca9864563?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>all generating comments</span></a><span> on PRs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Multi-agent code review.</span></strong><span> Build a custom solution which triggers several models/agents to review the code and suggest fixes.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Agents update PRs with fixes. </span></strong><span>Vendors and home-grown solutions can instruct agents to update PRs with fixes and then re-trigger reviews – if you trust agents to make sensible fixes, that is!</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Typical processes:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table cycle</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the above cases, engineers typically review the </span><em><span>review</span></em><span> itself, and not usually the code. Here’s Etienne Dilocker, cofounder and CTO at AI database software, Weaviate, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/45de9851-c862-4b0e-a0be-ee867761faeb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explaining</span></a><span> why he likes their approach:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong><span>It’s very hard for agents to get the balance [of the code review] right.</span></strong><span> If you ignore human code review entirely and leave it to agents, every PR will either suffer from scope creep or ship critical issues. But, of course, you can’t review everything by hand. So my current favorite setup is:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>1. an (adversarial) agent does a review</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>2. a human makes a scope decision</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>3. an agent implements the feedback</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>4. either repeat or break the loop (likely a human decision)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So basically, 90% is left to agents, with humans in the loop for critical scope decisions and exit criteria.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Noise is a  big problem with AI code reviews.</span></strong><span> WeTravel, a Series C travel tech company, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/636b3279-7df4-4d66-a36f-7e810ae20232?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>decided</span></a><span> to not use AI for code reviews because of the amount of noise it generated. In June, they did an updated evaluation which showed lots of improvement, but still not enough to justify adopting AI for the task.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As things stand, custom tooling is probably needed to reduce code-review noise. Uber built a clever approach for this; an agentic pipeline called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1c8a39f7-cb1a-47a8-8000-27a6744f3bd6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>uReview:</span></a></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Comments are graded, and low-confidence comments removed</span></p></li><li 0;"><span>Comments are merged, categorized, and unimportant ones removed</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>… in the end, the AI review results in important comments being shown to devs</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>2. Triage by “blast radius” & choose an approach</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another common approach is to decide whether to review code by hand or with AI, based on how “risky” a change is:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Low-risk change:</span></strong><span> only AI, without human review. It can ship to production once AI agents are happy</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>High-risk change: </span></strong><span>mandatory human review</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is the approach that Anthropic and OpenAI follow, which I confirmed by talking with both companies. At Anthropic, Jarred Sumner </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f16f2909-ebdb-47e2-909d-9da356b9b83c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>told me</span></a><span> that a human merges even low-risk changes, but that their goal is eventually to get another Claude instance to merge low-risk changes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And it’s not just at leading AI labs: five-person startup, Duckbill Group, a cloud and AI cost management company, changed their process, as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7159ef07-4cae-4985-a91d-3a61778ef73e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explained</span></a><span> by cofounder and CEO Mike Julian:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We ditched code review at Duckbill Group (mostly)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>About a month ago, we found ourselves with 60 open PRs for a team of five. They had been accumulating for a few weeks and we all had the sudden realization we were looking at two days of just code review.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I had been tossing around the idea for a while about having AI do all code review and so I just asked the team: what if we just didn’t review the PRs?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We decided to do a couple of things:</span></p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Switch to a risk-based system. </span></strong><span>With a risk-based system, we agreed that if your change touched the public API/MCP, auth, design system, non-additive database schema changes, or agent skills, it needed a human review. We then enforced that with a shell script to add a GitHub label.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Improve our guardrails</span></strong><span> (unit and end-to-end testing, post-deploy observability, stricter linting and type checking, etc). Improving guardrails was pretty easy, just expensive in tokens and attention. We enabled nearly every rule in ruff/prettier/eslint/ty, and we improved our unit test coverage to a floor of 85%.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Results before vs after:</span></p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>PRs merged: 353 → 684 (80/wk → 154/wk, +94%)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Merged within 1h: 28% → 45%; within 24h: 76% → 80%</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Human-reviewed PRs median merge time: 26h</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>No human-review median merge time: 1h.”</span></p></li></ul></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here’s how I’d visualize this approach:</span></p><div Review the plan/tests/database schema, but not the implementation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some devs and teams have stopped reviewing the code (the implementation), and instead review the “before” and “after” states:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Review the plan: </span></strong><span>spend a lot more time on the plan than before, to get a much more detailed spec. Using </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/056df39b-b6dd-4582-bb11-7f790bf6053c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The /grill-me skill</span></a><span> by Matt Pocock is a popular method, and I’m also a fan of it for thorough upfront planning, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/74c0bb31-b890-4b4f-9413-dc740853750f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>as is</span></a><span> Andrea Francesco Speziale, Principal Engineer at Musixmatch:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“After 3 hours of /grill-me, it better one-shot the implementation. I’m not spending a single minute on any review!”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Review the tests: </span></strong><span>via Test Driven Development (TDD) – which is much easier with agents when writing the tests upfront is a chore – or by focusing the review to ensure the software is tested.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One argument for this approach is that customers and users of software usually don’t care about the code. There’s a caveat that automated tests can verify a lot of different software – and are great at verifying business logic – but they don’t do a good job at verifying whether a UI </span><em><span>looks</span></em><span> and </span><em><span>feels </span></em><span>good.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Review the database schema. </span></strong><span>Jackie Luo, cofounder and CEO of AI startup Sigil, and formerly an engineer at Square, says:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“My current take is that all that really matters is the database schema. Speaking from a fast-moving startup perspective:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>1. Everything, besides data, is fluid and recoverable.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>2. The schema is the “hard” representation of what’s been built and reveals the riskiest changes, so it’s a good attention/impact tradeoff.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>3. Business logic only matters because product behavior matters—so ideally align on that before interacting with a coding agent at all. Then, once the code is written, use abstractions to understand any other significant decisions made.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Understand the product over the code. Use abstractions to translate the latter to the former – except in the case of schemas!”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Jackie’s point is that data (that is, the state) is the most “rigid” part of any system. Stateless business logic is now easy to change because it’s “just” code, and code is easy and fast to generate and regenerate. For startups, it’s worth getting the data schema – and thereby your state machine – right. Then, everything else will be easy and fast to iterate on.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>My sense is this approach makes perfect sense for a startup iterating to get product-market fit. However, once you have a business, you’ll want to “guard” the business logic with tests: else your product could break, and existing users will be unhappy when this happens!</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>4. Produce less code</span></h2><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What about simply not accepting a future in which agents produce more and longer PRs, more verbose code, and more code to review? Some teams enforce sensible rules for pull requests that existed before AI:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Keep them small: maximum 500 lines per pull request. If bigger, then open standalone PRs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Have a PR do only one thing: don’t mix scaffolding, adding of business logic, implementing two features in one PRs, etc</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Use </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0c221a0c-e36c-441d-9dec-6fb3f78b9872?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>stacked diffs</span></a><span>: mainstream tools like GitHub have added support, so keeping pull requests small is easier</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is where it helps for engineers to be more hands-on with agents; when you pay attention to what the AI does, you can stop it from implementing functionality from scratch when it could use an existing module or an existing library, for instance.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>5. Review everything by hand</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s worth pointing out that reviewing code “by hand” is far from entirely dead across the tech industry; indeed, some engineers and teams still swear by it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Building a better release process could still be more impactful than automating code review. </span></strong><span>This is what </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c5fc1ad5-567d-4686-8c5b-d737c66781cc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>George Salakirov</span></a><span>, VP of Product Engineering at WeTravel, told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We still do human code review, and use our ‘vanilla’ coding agents to generate code. While I see a potential for a good product with AI code review tools, the gains compared to us reviewing our own code still feel marginal with the current generation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In our case, building a good release process and moving over to a monorepo are both projects we expect to improve engineering productivity a lot more: so we’ve prioritized these, before we’d look into potential code review automations. We’re already seeing a lift from these investments in our developer productivity.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also, the gap seems to be closing when AI code review tools could be useful enough for us: and we re-evaluate available tools on the market every quarter.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Software engineer Dima Belyaev </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7376cc73-96a8-4ab7-88fe-a672453aaf82?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>also prefers</span></a><span> to review code by hand, even if it is “skimming”:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I’m still in the camp of code reviewing everything, even though we have agents doing that too. So far I’m only skimming through well-scoped internal changes as long as there is a working reproduction of the code (CI, internal docs etc).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I stopped reading tests in the PRs, though: I’m quite confident in their quality and fine if they’re more verbose than they could be, those tests are easy to fix later.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most of the AI code review tools test the product first, leaving architectural / API questions next, with clear understanding of which are easy fixes for an agent to apply vs which are questions for the author to make a decision / push back.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Most of my code review comments / questions these days</span></strong><span>: so in case an agent does another pass, they could explain the reason why it’s implemented this way and either have me agree or push back with more context and specific direction.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>It may turn out that regulation and compliance concerns preserve human code review from extinction, longer term. </span></strong><span>For example, some companies interpret security assessments like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2dd49600-84c4-4f3f-a5ae-f9c5b77d0643?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>FedRAMP</span></a><span> as requiring humans to review every single line of code that goes into production. However, FedRAMP itself doesn’t necessarily demand line-by-line human review: it’s down to the company and the auditor to agree on how to interpret the regulation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/885beae6-ea7f-4afa-b0e5-8fe89fb02773?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>PCI DSS</span></a><span>, human code review is mandatory when code review is the chosen review method, but it also allows other review techniques.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>6. No more human code review?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I expected to hear from engineers who have completely removed the human from the code review process, and that was the case.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The teams that I could confirm have ditched human code reviews for production software are early-stage, “AI-native” startups. </span></strong><span>For example, here is the cofounder of Glide, an AI spreadsheets startup, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/49afd425-ae5e-414b-942d-7c84cf8eea07?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explaining</span></a><span> their approach. Simon Fletcher says:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We went fully agentic around four months ago. The throughput gain has been significant, roughly 4.5x more PRs merged per month. The system’s state continues to hold up. Surprisingly, security and reliability are actually higher than when we had our human process in place. The agentic review allows us to have agents work on these toil tasks more autonomously.  I will admit, it does require guardrails and other forms of backpressure in the system to fully trust it.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Glide built an “agentic rollout pipeline” before throwing away human code review. This internal platform is called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d2e6d274-3051-49ed-a379-7639322a76b6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Slipstream</span></a><span>:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Tests and evals</span></strong><span>: these run after the AI code review, and have to pass for the next step to begin</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Human sign-off:</span></strong><span> Glide doesn’t deploy automatically to prod: a dev looks through the AI code review and CI results before greenlighting to deploy</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Agent “babysits” the deploy</span></strong><span>: using a feature flag, an agent gradually rolls out the change and checks for degradation in metrics, which are flagged in Slack</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here’s how Slipstream looks in action:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On one hand, I like agentic gradual rollout as an automation a lot! On the other, it involves a bunch more infrastructure work to make core reviews no longer mandatory. Also, when code reviews are no longer part of development, is there a risk of more tech debt making it into the codebase faster?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It will be interesting to see how the codebases and products of startups that go all-in on agentic code reviews, are holding up in 6-12 months’ time. </span><em><span>Regardless, I’m all for experimentation, and we see some neat experimentation by Glide!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Other incidences of complete automation I heard about were side projects, single-person businesses, or very early-stage startups with no product-market fit. Basically, places where shipping a broken prototype is not a big deal.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>7. Why do we review code, anyway?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’ve covered how teams are responding to ever more code being generated by AI which is correspondingly harder to review. At this point, it’s worth returning to fundamentals and considering </span><em><span>why</span></em><span> we do code review in the first place. It’s been a tech industry norm for decades, and long a mandatory part of the development process, but is it becoming pointless and redundant?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, with AI agents being able to do more than ever, the question arises of why people should be involved in the process; what are the benefits of not letting the AI tool do it all? From my perspective, the reasons for human code review are manifold:</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Technical reasons</span></h3><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Conversations about architecture. </span></strong><span>For better or worse, many architecture discussions take place within code reviews; such as about scaffolding or building new components, whether a method should belong to a class, or if a functionality be in a separate module, etc. This kind of debate is better to have during implementation than afterward; (although the optimal time would be even earlier!) </span><em><span>Of course, the reality of building software involves figuring out design details as the software is built.</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Missing tests / ignored conventions. </span></strong><span>In teams without lint rules on conventions or test coverage, code review comments can reveal when things are missing. Yes, automating this feedback is pretty trivial, but automated code review still remains far from great at deciding whether a test is good or was “written to pass.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Less tech debt.</span></strong><span> Code review is a great place for experienced engineers to call out shortcuts that add tech debt and need to be addressed before committing, or in an immediate follow-up review. Cases may include when a method gets overly complicated, or a dev adds more code to an already messy component in need of a cleanup.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Extra bug-catching layer. </span></strong><span>There’s often an expectation that code reviews will catch bugs; however, in my experience, code reviews have always been a poor line of defense against bugs by themselves. It is a benefit of human code reviews that an experienced engineer can sometimes spot obvious issues that would lead to problems. Still, catching bugs is better done by other means, like via a thorough test suite.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Nitpicking</span></strong><span>. Nitpicking can go too far when engineers add comments on minor, unimportant details which then trigger lengthy back-and-forth debates about variables not being in alphabetical order, or whether a variable name is the right length, etc. But within reason, nitpicking still forms part of healthy, robust debate on a team, unless it’s a symptom of other issues – see below.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Team reasons</span></h3><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Knowledge sharing and reducing the “bus factor.”</span></strong><span> By doing code reviews, team members learn how new code works, which is useful because they can take over the work, add to it, and fix issues when needed. This reduces the risk of a project failing or ceasing to work as people leave and move on from it; aka the ‘bus factor’.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Professional growth.</span></strong><span> For junior engineers, code review feedback from experienced devs is a professional growth opportunity. In my early career, I worked hard to not repeat the mistakes of past code reviews, and felt pride when a senior dev with a high code review bar said “good job” about a longer code change.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Cross-team collaboration. </span></strong><span>At companies with an “internal open source” model where anyone can raise pull requests against any part of the code, it’s a lot easier to raise a PR than to call a meeting with the other team, or raise a JIRA ticket. Comments on the pull request often turn into discussions about what the other team intends to do, and how they could do it better. It could lead to engineers starting to talk more to each other; for example, if a code review shows there was a misunderstanding.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Code review can reveal team dynamics. </span></strong><span>As a manager, I found that a good way to spot conflict and frustrations among team members was in code reviews, such as excessive nitpicking, passive-aggressive language, or when normally-quiet devs started commenting a lot on others’ coding efforts. Reviews enabled me to detect conflicts early and then talk with devs to figure out if there was a problem (there usually was!) With AI code reviews, does intra-team conflict disappear, or is it just less obvious? I don’t know, but it will surely create </span><em><span>new</span></em><span> dynamics to deal with.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Organizational reasons</span></h3><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Create accountability and traceability. </span></strong><span>Signing off a code change creates accountability, as it’s not just the engineer who wrote the code who is accountable, but also the person who signed it off. It’s not uncommon during code freezes to only allow code that’s been signed off by a Staff+ or Director+ level to be deployed, when stability matters more than speed. Also, code reviews make it easy to know who saw and approved the code going out.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Compliance and governance. </span></strong><span>Some code reviews are mandated at regulated companies; for example, a security team might need to do a mandatory security review of critical parts of the codebase in order to follow an internal process.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In many cases above, code review could be replaced or augmented with another layer, and the process of catching bugs could be more effective with a thorough test suite, or via dogfooding, running the system inside a hostile simulation before deploying, or monitoring in production. Of course, today an argument can be made for AI tools as a replacement, but that necessarily comes at the cost of some of what makes human-centered code review useful in teams and orgs.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Takeaways</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As engineers, we’ve pretty swiftly moved to allow AI agents to generate the code, but reviewing that code doesn’t yet seem a responsibility that can be easily delegated to AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Right now, there are a few reasons for this; AI code review tools tend to be too noisy, and many professionals simply don’t trust them sufficiently for the task, as things stand. As software engineers, we’re paid to solve problems of the business and its customers. There’s a well-established process for this: understand the problem → make a plan → write the code → validate that it works → ship to production → ensure it keeps working.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>By delegating the writing of code to an AI agent, we make ourselves one step removed from the code itself. In this case, it only makes sense to spend more time on either specifying it upfront (places which spend more time planning or on database schemas) or validating it (with test suites or code reviews).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I admit that reviewing code has never been my favorite activity as it’s not creative like building software is, and I wonder how close we’ll be able to stay to the code after many of us stop writing it. If it is only a matter of time until agents have more feedback loops to confirm that code works as expected, then devs will spend most of our time specifying what to build, but then not actually building it. In that scenario, our role will be to just review that things “feel” right after the fact.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>These changes are unfolding in real time, and I’m interested to hear from you about it. Comment below on how code review is changing in your team or company? What is the good and bad of relying ever more on AI code review, and how far can this approach be pushed today?</span></em></p><p class="button-wrapper" How To Be Direct And Strategic

Yue Zhao

"I saw an issue with a process on my team recently and brought it up directly in a team meeting a few days later. I was very direct about the problem, gave all the details, and explained how it impacted everyone. To my surprise, my manager shut it down completely, and now I cannot get any buy-in from anyone. What happened? Where did I do wrong?"

#Leadership Communication

#Management Productivity AI

But there is one major difference. Apart from normal processing, the application also sends data to a large language model (LLM). It then uses the model’s response to carry out a task. For example, a customer support chatbot might depend on an LLM to answer user queries. A document-processing system can use an LLM to extract names, dates, and invoice amounts from the uploaded documents. A coding assistant might ask an LLM to write a piece of code and integrate it into the logical flow.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On face value, we might feel that building such an application is quite simple:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The user sends a request.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The application sends a prompt to an LLM.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The LLM returns an answer.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The application displays that answer or uses the same for some other processing.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, there are chances that any of these steps can fail. The network might be unavailable. The LLM provider might reject the user request for various reasons. The request might go through, but the model might return invalid JSON. The LLM can misunderstand the instructions and invent false information due to hallucinations. They might also take a long time to respond.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The techniques for resiliency and error handling help prepare the application to handle these situations in the best possible manner.
