0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Meaning of Error Handling and Resiliency</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before we get into the details, let us understand what error handling and resiliency exactly mean.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You can think of error handling as a part of the program responsible for deciding the appropriate action when something goes wrong. For example, consider an application that calls an LLM API. If the request is successful, the program processes the response in a normal way. But if it fails, the program might have to choose from various options, such as retrying the request, showing an explanatory message, using a backup model, or recording the failure for further investigation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Any of these approaches is much better than allowing the entire application to crash. But we also cannot treat every problem in the same manner. A real production application should be able to distinguish between different types of failures so that we can take the right action. Therefore, good error handling needs an understanding of what failed and why.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In contrast, resiliency is an application’s ability to continue doing its job even when some parts of the system are failing. We don’t need an application to operate perfectly to be resilient. Failures are fine. But they should happen in a controlled manner. This is also known as graceful degradation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, consider a travel assistant that uses an LLM to build personalized itineraries for travellers. If the primary LLM it depends on is unavailable, the application can use a smaller backup model for creating the itineraries. If that model also becomes unavailable, the application can display previously created destination guides for the same locations. Of course, these answers won’t be personalized, but the user won’t just see a useless error message.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While error handling deals with an individual failure, resiliency is more concerned about the behavior of the entire system even when things are failing.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Why do LLM Applications Need Special Treatment for Error Handling?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Traditional software apps work according to well-defined rules. If we write a function that adds 5 and 7, it will always return 12. If the function returns successfully, the result is deemed valid.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With LLMs, we don’t have this luxury. This is because the output from LLMs is probabilistic. In other words, the same prompt can produce different answers every single time. Also, a successful API request to an LLM doesn’t guarantee that the response we receive is correct or even usable. For all we know, the response might be utterly gibberish. This means that an LLM API call might appear successful based on status code, but it might be a failure in logical terms. There are several things that could be wrong with the response:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The model might have ignored some part of the instructions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It might have returned a pure text response when the application expected JSON.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The LLM might hallucinate and invent a product, policy, or piece of information that has no basis in real data.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The model might return an incomplete response because it reached its token limit.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The LLM can refuse a harmless request because it misunderstood the context.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The LLM might select the wrong tool or call a tool with invalid arguments.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Lastly, the LLM might return an answer that violates some important business rule.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We can broadly notice two categories of failures over here:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Technical Failures: </span></strong><span>They happen when the system can’t even complete the operation. This involves stuff like network errors, timeouts, unavailable service, invalid credentials, and so on.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Semantic Failures: </span></strong><span>These types of failures show up even when the operation is technically successful. But the result might be incorrect, unsafe, irrelevant, or even unusable.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Conventional error handling focuses on dealing with technical failures. However, LLM-powered applications need to handle both technical and semantic failures.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Does a Request Flow in an LLM-powered App?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LLM-powered apps contain much more than an LLM. We have many different components that come together to make an application complete. See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/a2f65095-e983-4bae-849e-27ad771a7ea3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/f734b2ff-1f7f-4c07-a7da-0955c6fd1ab6_2048x1214.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":863,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="325.9958791208791" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!u90q!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff734b2ff-1f7f-4c07-a7da-0955c6fd1ab6_2048x1214.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As an example, consider a shopping chatbot that checks products based on the user’s preference. It first runs a search on a product database and gives the results back to an LLM. It then asks the model to select the right products for a particular user and then calls an inventory API to find out the availability of those products.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We can have failures at every boundary within this application. The user might provide some invalid information. The product search may return no results. The request to the LLM might time out due to external reasons. The model may return an unknown product identifier. The inventory service might go down. Lastly, even if the response is somehow generated, it might be interrupted while streaming to the user.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To make an application truly resilient, we can’t treat the LLM as an isolated component. We need to consider the path of the request from the beginning to the end and identify potential problems.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Main Types of Errors and Failures</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us now look at the main types of errors and failures that can occur in such an application.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Invalid User Input</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some failures can show up even before the LLM is called. For example, a user may submit an empty message, upload an unacceptable file format, provide an extremely large document, or enter an invalid date.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In such cases, the application should be able to validate obvious requirements. There is no need to call an LLM to find out if a mandatory email address is missing or if an uploaded file exceeds the size limit. If we reject invalid requests early, we can save time and processing costs. We can also provide much clearer error messages to the users since the rules are fixed.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Network and Connection Failures</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An application talks to an LLM provider over the internet. However, the connections can be interrupted. We can have DNS lookup failures. Responses might be lost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Such type of failures are temporary. We can retry the request. But the application cannot retry indefinitely. We also need to consider whether it is safe to repeat the operation and whether there are any unforeseen side effects.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Timeouts</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this case, the LLM may take longer to respond than the application can wait. If there’s no timeout, the request can remain stuck while consuming resources.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The timeout value defines how long the application can wait. For example, an interactive chat application might have a timeout of 20 seconds. But an offline document-analysis job might allow several minutes. Also, the timeout should depend on the user experience. For example, a user waiting on a screen should have a shorter deadline than a background task that runs overnight.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Rate Limits</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LLM providers have a limit to how many requests or tokens a specific account can use within a time period. If the application goes above this limit, the LLM provider may return a rate-limit error. This is represented by the HTTP status code 429.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Getting a rate limit response doesn’t mean that the service is broken. It means that our application is making more requests than what the provider can handle at a given point in time. To handle this, the application may need to delay the requests, reduce concurrency, put the work in a queue, or switch to another model that might have available capacity.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Provider and Server Failures</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In certain situations, the LLM provider might be down due to a temporary internal problem. These failures are commonly represented by HTTP 5xx status codes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this case, a limited retry attempt could be a good idea because the failure might vanish quickly. However, if the failures continue, repeated retry calls only increase the load upon an already struggling service. is reasonable because the failure may disappear quickly. The application should stop retrying and switch to an alternative execution path if possible.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Authentication and Permission Failures</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If the application provides an expired or invalid API key, it might also result in a 401 or 403 response from the LLM provider.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this case, there is very little point to retrying. The application should record the failure, alert the relevant parties, and return an appropriate message to the user. It must take care not to expose API keys or other internal security details to the user.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Context-length Failures</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every language model has a limit on how much text it can process in one request. The prompt, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool definitions, and expected answer are all part of this context window and consume space.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If the application sends a lot of information to the LLM, the LLM may reject the request, or it may have too little space for the answer. An application designed with resiliency in mind usually counts tokens before sending the request. It can also remove old conversation messages, summarize earlier content, retrieve fewer documents, or divide a large job into smaller pieces to stay within the limit.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Malformed or Unexpected Output</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s say our application expects a result in the following format.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>{</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “customer_name”: “Adam Smith”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “priority”: “high”</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>}</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, the model might reply something like: “The customer’s name appears to be Adam Smith, and this looks urgent.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Such an answer might make sense to a human being, but the application that expects a JSON response can’t process it. To get around this, the application should use a structured-output feature if the model provider supports it. It should also validate the response against a schema before using it.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Incorrect or Invented Information</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The most dangerous LLM failures happen in the form of plausible answers that are completely wrong. This occurs due to model hallucination.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, a customer-support assistant might invent a refund policy that doesn’t exist. A research tool might generate a source that doesn’t exist. An inventory assistant might recommend a product that is not even there in the catalog.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Such problems can’t be detected by catching exceptions because no technical exception occurred. To handle these types of issues, the application needs additional checks, trusted data sources, or some form of human intervention to proceed further.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Tool Failures and Partial Completion</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LLMs are also now used as agents that can make API calls, search databases, send messages, or perform transactions. This gives rise to a major problem. The specific action taken by the LLM might succeed even when the surrounding workflow fails.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, suppose the LLM assistant calls a payment service. The payment succeeds, but the network connection breaks before the application gets the confirmation. If the application retries the payment blindly, we might end up charging the customer twice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is the reason tool-based systems need idempotency, state tracking, and recovery mechanisms.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How to Classify Failures to Take Appropriate Action</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So how do we deal with all these different types of errors in an LLM-powered application?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The first step is to classify them. There are main categories:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A transient error is temporary and usually disappears if we attempt the operation again. For example, network problems, rate limits, and server failures.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A permanent error continues until there is a change in the request or the system. Such errors include invalid credentials, unsupported file types, permission issues, and malformed requests.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A semantic error occurs when the response is technically correct, but doesn’t solve the application’s requirements. Examples are invalid JSON, unsupported tool arguments, hallucinations, and so on.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Once we are able to classify an error, we can deal with it appropriately. For a transient error, we should retry after a short delay or use a fallback. For permanent errors, we need to report to the concerned parties who can correct the problem. For semantic errors, we need to validate, repair, or request human review.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, not every error also fits neatly into a single category. For example, a context-length error is permanent for the current prompt. However, it can be solved by making the prompt shorter.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How To Retry a Request Correctly?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us look at some techniques to deal with failures. The first one to check out is retrying a request.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Retries are one of the simplest ways to improve an application’s resiliency. If an operation fails because of a brief network problem, chances are that it will work fine once the application waits for a while and tries again.</span></p><div used for timeouts, temporary network failures, 429 responses, and some specific 5xx responses. We shouldn’t use them for failures such as invalid credentials, prohibited requests, bad input, or other problems that will produce the same result every single time.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How to Manage Fallbacks and Graceful Degradation?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In an application, the fallback path is an alternative path. It is used when the normal preferred path fails due to some failure.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An application can use the fallback approach in the following manner:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Attempt to use the primary model, which is usually of high quality.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>If that model is unavailable, switch to a smaller backup model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>If no model is available, return a pre-defined fallback response or cached information.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Lastly, if the request can’t be handled safely through any option, transfer it to a human for further action.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 approach depends on the task. For example, we might be okay to use a smaller model for summarizing an internal meeting. However, it might not be a good choice for interpreting a complicated legal document. Similarly, a cached response may be good enough for a general FAQ type scenario. But it won’t be suitable for something like the current account balance.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In other words, the fallback strategy should not violate the original requirements of the operation. We can’t just plug any available model into the flow. It’s also important to avoid dependency on a single point of failure. For example, if both the primary and backup models are accessed through the same provider, an outage can disable both. For real redundancy, we should have separation between the two pathways.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Do Circuit Breakers Work in this Setup?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider a scenario where the LLM provider is unavailable. Every request is timing out. In such cases, it is not wise to keep sending more requests. They only waste resources and make users wait for failures.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A circuit breaker can temporarily stop calls to a failing service. It commonly has three states:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In the closed state, we can send the requests at normal cadence.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In the open state, requests get rejected or redirected immediately. This is because the service is considered unhealthy.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In the half-open state, a small number of test requests are allowed to go through. They help determine whether the service has recovered to some extent.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: requests in the half-open state succeed, the circuit can close. But if they fail, the circuit goes back to the open state. In this way, circuit breakers help get rid of repeated failures from infecting the rest of the application. They also let us configure the appropriate fallback behaviour.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Rate Limiting, Queues, and Concurrency Control</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An LLM-powered application can’t accept unlimited LLM work just because users can submit it from the UI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, if 10K requests arrive at once, forwarding all of them to the LLM provider immediately might exhaust provider limits, database connections, memory, or the application’s budget.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Using rate limiting, we can control how frequently a user or client can submit requests. With concurrency control, we can limit how frequently a user or client might submit requests. Also, concurrency control puts a cap on how many requests the application can process simultaneously. A queue stores extra work until capacity becomes available.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Interactive requests where a user is waiting for the response should usually receive higher priority over background work. For example, a user waiting for a chat response should not be blocked because thousands of documents are being summarized in the background.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The application should also place limits on token usage, document size, number of retrieved passages, number of tool calls, and total workflow duration.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we have taken a detailed look at resiliency and error handling aspects when it comes to LLM-powered applications.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The key takeaway is that LLM-powered applications can have failures that are different from traditional applications. This is because of the inherent probabilistic approach of the LLMs. The important thing is to classify the type of failure so that proper action can be taken by the application.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Despite the differences in the types of errors, we can still borrow many of the techniques for error handling from traditional applications. item.title: The startup's Postgres survival guide
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The startup's Postgres survival guide

Alexander Belanger

14 minutes by Alexander Belanger Alexander shares practical lessons from running Postgres in a growing startup. He explains how to design schemas, write efficient queries, manage connections, handle migrations, and tune autovacuum. He also covers query planning, batching, partitioning, locking, and large data migrations. The goal is to help engineers keep Postgres fast, reliable, and stable as their applications scale.
item.description: The startup's Postgres survival guide

item.title: simple terms
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
simple terms

Nadeem Shaikh

4 minutes by Nadeem Shaikh Oracle's Orasort algorithm compares 8 bytes at a time by converting string chunks into 64-bit integers, instead of the traditional one byte at a time approach. This reduces CPU cycles and makes sorting up to 5 times faster. After its patent expired in 2024, open-source databases like MySQL and PostgreSQL began adopting it, and cloud companies now benefit from lower computing costs.
item.description: simple terms

item.title: Fornax's guide to ridiculously fast ethernet
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Fornax's guide to ridiculously fast ethernet

Wim

28 minutes by Wim Getting a 100 Gbps server to actually run at full speed takes serious tuning across the entire system. Key Linux network settings need adjusting, including TCP buffer sizes, congestion control, and memory limits. The network card also needs careful configuration through ethtool, covering ring buffers and interrupt timing. Critically, disabling the IOMMU in the BIOS often makes the biggest difference, yet almost no guides mention it. Cores in space: The core memory module from a 1980 Spacelab
item.description: Fornax's guide to ridiculously fast ethernet

item.title: computer
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
computer

Ken Shirriff

25 minutes by Ken Shirriff Spacelab, a reusable lab carried in the Space Shuttle's cargo bay, used a French-built computer with 128 kilobytes of magnetic core memory instead of modern semiconductor chips. Core memory stores each bit in a tiny magnetic ring, which can hold data without power and resists radiation, making it ideal for space use. Built in 1980, this was an advanced late-era core memory system using high-density components and a design that boosted performance by removing the need for inhibit wires. Semiconductor memory eventually replaced it in the 1990s.
item.description: computer

item.title: Parity before cutover
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Parity before cutover

Alex O'Callaghan

3 minutes by Alex O'Callaghan Big rewrites held back from production let risk build up silently. Bugs pile up, fixes get missed, and two versions drift apart until a painful cutover reveals everything at once. Downgrading to an older Python version first made it possible to run one codebase in both old and new infrastructure, so each migration step changed only one thing. By the time the cloud switch happened, it was uneventful. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Parity before cutover

item.title: How to make AI write high-quality code in .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to make AI write high-quality code in .NET

Anton Martyniuk

AI can write .NET code quickly, but it does not always follow your coding standards. Anton explains how to make AI-generated code more reliable using build rules, static analyzers and centralized package management. He shows how to use separate AI code reviews and Claude skills to catch clean-code issues before human review. The goal is to make your standards enforceable instead of relying on prompts. See one of the few solutions purpose-built for generating real
item.description: How to make AI write high-quality code in .NET

item.title: System.Text.Json
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
System.Text.Json

Andrew Lock

.NET 11 and C# 15 are adding support for both union types and closed class hierarchies. In this post, Andrew looks at how System.Text.Json handles these new type hierarchies, the differences between them, as well as some of the sharp edges to watch out for.
item.description: System.Text.Json

item.title: Nullable GUID route constraints in ASP.NET Core
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Nullable GUID route constraints in ASP.NET Core

Sebastian Nilsson

ASP.NET Core has a built-in GUID route constraint, so no custom code is needed. Add guid to a route parameter to block non-GUID URLs from reaching your endpoint, and add `?` to make the parameter optional. These constraints only control which endpoint gets selected, not whether the value is valid for your business logic, so always validate that separately inside your endpoint. Signal shingle: A novel architecture for high-performance ASP.NET
item.description: Nullable GUID route constraints in ASP.NET Core

item.title: multi-widget sites
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
multi-widget sites

Scott Galloway

Dashboards look like one page but trigger many expensive database calls per visitor, and the problem multiplies fast under load. Signal Shingle solves this by pre-rendering each widget as a cached fragment derived from a single generation-stamped data model, so responses read from cache rather than starting fresh database work. A separate scheduled process handles refresh within a measurable cost budget, meaning heavy traffic makes the system do less work, not more. The page stays fast and coherent even when data is slightly older, and the age is always shown honestly.
item.description: multi-widget sites

item.title: Generate and review the public API of a .NET library
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Generate and review the public API of a .NET library

Gérald Barré

Meziantou.Framework.PublicApiGenerator creates a readable C# file showing the library’s public surface, making API changes easier to spot and review. The tool supports multiple target frameworks, modern .NET 11 features, and CI validation, helping developers detect accidental breaking changes before they reach users. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Generate and review the public API of a .NET library

0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In consistent hashing, you distribute data across different machines or servers using a virtual circular ring.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>PubSub is an asynchronous messaging pattern that decouples service creators from service consumers.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In circuit breaker distributed pattern, it stops an application from repeatedly executing an operation that is likely to fail.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In Retry with a backoff pattern, you handle temporary network glitches or brief service timeouts. It is a resiliency pattern. </span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In the leader election pattern, you designate a single master node to manage actions and maintain cluster state. It’s what stops two nodes from thinking they’re in charge.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In quorum read/write pattern, you ensure enough replicas agree on each read and write so that the set overlaps. It is a data consistency pattern that is used in distributed databases to guarantee up-to-date information.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Saga is a design pattern that manages distributed transactions through a sequence of local transactions across multiple microservices. machine runs a complete operating system, Windows, Fedora, or Ubuntu, with its own kernel, drivers, and libraries. The hypervisor (VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM) sits directly on hardware and emulates physical machines for each guest OS.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;">This makes VMs heavy but isolated. No separate OS per container. Just isolated processes with their own filesystem and dependencies.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;">The container engine (Docker, containerd, CRI-O, Podman) manages lifecycle, networking, and isolation, but it all runs on top of a single shared kernel. Lightweight and fast. Containers start in milliseconds because you’re not booting an OS, just launching a process.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;">But here’s the catch: all containers on a host must be compatible with that host’s kernel. auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When you open a website, the difference between HTTP and HTTPS decides whether your data travels safely or in plain sight. Here’s what actually happens under the hood:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">HTTP:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Sends data in plain text, anyone on the network can intercept it.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The client and server perform a simple TCP handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Fast but completely insecure. Passwords, tokens, and forms can all be read in transit.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">HTTPS (SSL/TLS):</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Step 1: TCP Handshake: Standard connection setup.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;">Step 2: Certificate Check: Client says hello. Server responds with hello and its SSL/TLS certificate. That certificate contains the server’s public key and is signed by a trusted Certificate Authority.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;">Your browser verifies this certificate is legitimate, not expired, and actually belongs to the domain you’re trying to reach. This proves you’re talking to the real server, not some attacker pretending to be it.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;">Step 3: Key Exchange: Here’s where asymmetric encryption happens. The server has a public key and a private key. Client generates a session key, encrypts it with the server’s public key, and sends it over. Only the server can decrypt this with its private key.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;">Both sides now have the same session key that nobody else could have intercepted. This becomes the symmetric encryption key for the rest of the session.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Step 4: Data Transmission: Now every request and response gets encrypted with that session key using symmetric encryption.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;">Over to you: What’s your go-to tool for debugging TLS issues, openssl, curl -v, or something else?</p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><table item.title: The Rise Of The End-To-End Operator
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Rise Of The End-To-End Operator

Wes Kao

“At all types of organizations, I’m seeing more high-performers get rewarded when they can handle projects end-to-end. If a normal operator is an infantry soldier, these operators are Navy SEALs. They can parachute into unknown territory to quickly assess a situation. Then determine the best course of action.”

#CareerGrowth
item.description: The Rise Of The End-To-End Operator

item.title: Load-Bearing People
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Load-Bearing People

Mike Fisher

“Pick your most critical system, process or relationship and name the one person holding it up. Then ask what happens if that person is unreachable for a month starting tomorrow. If the answer scares you, write it down before the feeling passes, because these risks survive on the decision to think about it later.”

#Management TeamHealth
item.description: Load-Bearing People

item.title: The Art Of Simplifying Decisions
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Art Of Simplifying Decisions

David Pereira

“For too long, we’ve endured complex decision-making approaches. Now that decisions are clearly our bottleneck, I’m bullish on those who can simplify them. I want to share my approach with you, and how you can bring it to your scenario. I hope this helps you simplify what others complicate.”

#Leadership DecisionMaking
item.description: The Art Of Simplifying Decisions

item.title: The Mistakes You're Allowed To Make
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Mistakes You're Allowed To Make

Steve Huynh

My friend said something to me once that I’ve been repeating ever since: “Bad news delivered early is just called news.” I think about that line every time I make a mistake.

#Communication CareerGrowth
item.description: The Mistakes You're Allowed To Make

item.title: The Safest Job From AI May Be Writing
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Safest Job From AI May Be Writing

Murat Demirbas

While the programmer's job description is getting completely refactored, writing remains surprisingly unaffected. LLMs have gotten very good at generating code, but I am appalled at the absolute shit they spew as prose... I am increasingly convinced LLMs will not threaten decent writers anytime soon. My prediction rests on the three observations below. Tell me where my logic does not hold up.

#AI CareerGrowth
item.description: The Safest Job From AI May Be Writing

item.title: Let's Build A Compressor From Scratch
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Let's Build A Compressor From Scratch

Adolfo Ochagavía

“Compression is one of those wonderful things we have grown accustomed to in the computer world. You wave a magic wand and — poof! — a file suddenly shrinks to a fraction of its size! You wave the wand again and — pop!— the original file is restored down to the last bit. How can this possibly work? Let’s find out!”

#DeepDive Algo
item.description: Let's Build A Compressor From Scratch

item.title: Building Autonomous Goal Loops That Deliver
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Building Autonomous Goal Loops That Deliver

Jarred Kenny

“The agent keeps moving, but movement is not the problem. The tests only protect what we already know, and the important failures sit outside them. A screen can look complete while it stores nothing. An agent can give the right answer for the wrong reason. A scorer can reward behavior no user wants. More turns make each of those failures cheaper and faster.”

#Testing AI Agents
item.description: Building Autonomous Goal Loops That Deliver

Here’s what CEO William Ready said (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Our approach to model deployment includes our own compact fit-for-purpose models built for Pinterest-specific use cases and suitable open source models post-trained in our own environment within our secure cloud infrastructure. When we leverage open source models, such as with Pinterest Assistant, we are seeing superior performance for our use cases when compared to closed third-party models because we are able to post-train open models on our highly unique data.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>With open models, we are achieving cost per transaction at less than 8% of the cost of comparable closed proprietary models. </span></strong><span>This gives us substantial headroom to deepen and extend these capabilities over time in a way that is differentiated, highly effective, and cost efficient.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Basically, what used to cost Pinterest $100 to run on a closed, frontier model, they now spend $8 on by using open models on owned or rented inference!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>AT&T: 56% savings by swapping Claude for open models</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With 100,000 employees, AT&T is a big spender on AI. The telco giant cut its AI bill by 56% while measuring a 2% decrease in the quality of AI’s output, after they moved workloads over to open models. From </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/10153f47-8aff-4d49-b647-cbd17236b0e8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The Information</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Austin said he’s found that open source models are “just as good or better” than older models sold by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI. For instance, AT&T’s software developers still rely on cutting-edge models for complex tasks like generating code, but can use cheaper open source models for less intense tasks like generating summaries of previously submitted code, he said.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After the company began using router provider LiteLLM, the costs of some advanced AI tasks such as coding fell by as much as 56% while the quality of the AI’s performance fell just 2%, Austin said.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Anthropic overpriced compared to the rest of the market?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Only a few months ago, Anthropic was the preferred model (Claude) and harness (Claude Code) among engineers. But Anthropic’s models are becoming steeply more expensive at a time when open weight models – and also OpenAI – are getting much cheaper. Meanwhile, Opus 5 is 100x more expensive (!!) than models like GPT-5.6 Luna xhigh and DeepSeek. That may be simply too much to ignore for some tech companies:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure 1);"><span>2. Automatic software maintenance experiments by Linear and Anthropic</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two interesting experiments took place involving getting agents to automate some parts of maintenance:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Karri Saarinen, cofounder at Linear </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a31aeccb-a872-47cd-9c38-b984e9890a25?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>shared</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Our bug autofix loop in Linear has fixed 300+ bugs in the last 30 days.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The team set it up as part of triage: it connects to Datadog and Sentry to investigate issues, then assigns them to Linear’s coding agent to fix.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Elsewhere, Boris Cherny, creator of Claude Code, is also </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/59bc3134-9655-486c-9c50-494866a8af0b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>experimenting</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“A weird experiment I’ve been trying the last few weeks is having Claude take over day-to-day maintenance of our apps. Seeing early signs of life that this might be possible.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The setup is straightforward: we have a Slack channel called proj-claude-maintains-apps. In it, Claude Tag runs a bunch of daily routines across iOS, Android, Desktop, web, CLI, and Agent SDK:</span></p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Crash fuzzer: open the app in a simulator and tap around to find ways to crash it, then root cause and fix the crashes</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Dup unifier: scans the codebase for similar-yet-slightly-divergent abstractions, and puts up PRs to unify them</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Dead-code remover: removes statically unreachable code, and adds logging to suspected dead code to check if it’s really dead and if so, remove it the next day</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Abstraction police: fixes leaky abstractions</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A bunch more..</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Results have been surprisingly positive. Over the last few weeks, these routines have opened 388 PRs across our repos, 180 of which we merged after Claude Code Review + human review. We’re now thinking about how to streamline this to make merging these kinds of mechanical changes easier.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In each case, the opening of PRs is automated and engineers decide whether or not to merge it. For Anthropic, 45% of PRs raised were worthy of merging. This doesn’t mean we’re close to “maintenance on autopilot”, but agents automatically raising PRs for bugs or maintenance tasks, is something that would have looked like science fiction even two years ago!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3.
