0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/59b8fb6b-f36b-4dbc-a9f4-44bd5700d5fe?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Amp</span></a><span>: supports GPT-5.6 or Fable 5.1 models, does not support Gemini</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>… and, until recently, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8ae7727c-c667-42c1-b07a-94c8a5e393e8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Cursor</span></a><span>, which supported GPT-5.6, Opus/Sonnet/Fable 5, and Gemini models</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This week, however, OpenAI announced the removal of GPT-5.6 from Cursor, effective November. Tibo Sottiaux, heading up Codex, explained (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We unfortunately have decided that we cannot continue providing access to our models through Cursor and are ending our partnership. </span><strong><span>It boils down to trust </span></strong><span>and we’ve asked that this takes effect on November 12 to give you some time to plan.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As a rule, frontier AI labs don’t like it when their cutting-edge models end up inside a rival’s product, supporting its success. For example,</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>OpenAI’s GPT models cannot be used from Anthropic’s Claude Code, or from Google’s Antigravity</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Anthropic’s Claude cannot be used with OpenAI’s Codex, out-of-the-box (even though Codex supports using other models when you bring your own API key), and Google’s Antigravity only offers seven month-old Claude models (Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6, which are considered so outdated that even Anthropic does not offer these anymore)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Google’s Gemini cannot be used from Claude Code or Codex (unless using it via API, in Codex)</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI announced this change right after SpaceX acquired Cursor and cited trust as the problem. In a longer, official statement, OpenAI </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c54140a5-b201-4823-8f48-8a53eba9fc48?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>spells it out</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We are making this choice because we cannot be confident that SpaceX will use our technology within our terms of service, based on our experience with Elon Musk’s companies violating contracts.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI has a point, as Elon Musk is known for acting as if legally binding contracts don’t apply to him: he just breaks them and forces the other party to sue for damages, which might take years. For example, when the world’s first trillionaire bought Twitter in 2022 and laid off 75% of employees, he refused to pay people’s contracted severance. Thousands of folks owed severance had to launch a class-action lawsuit in 2023, which lasted three years. X </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8452470b-7406-46c3-9ffe-997bfdf3d9f2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>finally settled</span></a><span> for only </span><em><span>almost</span></em><span> the previously legally due amount! People fought three years in court to win </span><em><span>less</span></em><span> severance than they were due. Perhaps Musk’s disdain for the law was rational after all!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was a fairly typical case of his way of doing business, so it’s unsurprising that OpenAI assumes SpaceX may not heed terms and conditions in the future about not using GPT-5.6 outputs to train its own next-generation model. That’s not allowed, but when did that stop the SpaceX owner from doing anything?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Interestingly, Anthropic has not pulled Claude from Cursor, but Anthropic is dependent on SpaceX for infra. </span></strong><span>To me, OpenAI pulling GPT from Cursor is a clear story. I was confused as to why Anthropic did not follow: because a year ago, the AI company cut off Claude usage for Windsurf, after rumors of OpenAI buying Windsurf were floating around. As TechCrunch reported at the time:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Anthropic co-founder and Chief Science Officer Jared Kaplan said his company cut Windsurf’s direct access to Anthropic’s Claude AI models largely because of rumors and reports that OpenAI, its largest competitor, is acquiring the AI coding assistant.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I think it would be odd for us to be selling Claude to OpenAI,” Kaplan said.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As a kicker: Windsurf was not bought by OpenAI – Google acquired the company instead. So Anthropic was decisive in cutting access based on a rumor. And yet, with SpaceX acquiring Cursor, Anthropic is content with a major frontier lab (SpaceX) offering Claude. This is surely because Anthropic is paying $15B per year to SpaceX to use their Colossus 1 data center, which provides critical compute to Anthropic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s rare to see a frontier lab like SpaceX have so much leverage over the leading AI lab, Anthropic: and given that Elon Musk is someone who is hard to trust in business, I assume Anthropic is looking for a way out of this awkward situation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the meantime, I’m sure Anthropic won’t be offended, should SpaceX not follow Claude’s own terms and conditions, especially on the anti-distillation clauses!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. HR tech startup operates with a “one dev per project” approach</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9a0c2354-43b0-485c-8121-8851ccadc83e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>reported</span></a><span> recently how projects at Anthropic are now done with a maximum of two software engineers, and one startup is taking this a step further with its one-dev-per-project model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ashby, a Series D HR tech company with around 70 engineers, also has zero deadlines and no standups, according to cofounder and VP of Engineering, Abhik Pramanik, who </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/abcdccdc-67d2-49e5-892d-46b29d1d8aab?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explained</span></a><span> how things work there:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Project teams of one engineer</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Engineers make both product and design decisions</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Engineers own features from product spec through launch</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>No standups, no JIRA tickets, no deadlines, no estimates</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Project teams which consist of one person at Ashby are clearly a result of AI tooling: a backend engineer, a frontend engineer and a designer are no longer needed to ship a new feature that touches the service layer, the frontend, and that looks decent.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, early-stage, VC-funded startups worked in similar ways pre-AI before product-market fit was found. Once it was, deadlines let customers know when to expect key launches. Ashby has definitely found product-market fit: it has more than 2,700 businesses paying for its recruitment platform, an Applicant Tracking System (ATS), and keeps iterating on it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>I also wonder if “no deadlines” is a good fit for most SaaS businesses. </span></strong><span>A software-as-a-service (SaaS) platform needs to keep up with how the industry operates and evolves, and keep solving the pain points customers have. When completing a project takes days instead of months, then why bother with deadlines?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Deadlines work best when used sparingly for major projects. I reckon Ashby does use – or will use – deadlines for either projects like a new product line, or when there’s an external deadline like a major event with a partner, an important sales demo for a large potential customer, etc.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7e1768cd-0883-4eb2-97d8-94561c598a28?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>interview</span></a><span> with NextPlay reports that the startup looks for the following skills:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Autonomy</span></strong><span>: own your work, end-to-end, and don’t be someone who depends on a PM to write tickets on what to do</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Great written communication skills</span></strong><span>: and knowing when and how to communicate with colleagues, usually in writing (since they’re all heads down, building projects with a bunch of agents)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Comfortable working full remote with few interactions</span></strong><span>: People who value social interaction highly are likely not a good fit, as the setup is remote and disincentivizes meetings.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s good to see full-remote companies like Ashby thrive. Full-remote work culture comes at the cost of less collaboration and conversation, but some people thrive in this environment!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>5. Industry Pulse</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Meta moved over to Slack for better agent interoperability</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are some eye-catching details in reports that Meta dropped Google Chat in favor of Slack because Google Chat has essentially no agentic capabilities, whereas Slack is excellent at integrating with AI agents. There’s a lot to unpack:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Meta used Google Chat?? </span></strong><span>Meta built its own internal chat tool called Workplace Chat, which has been used for close to a decade. But as I previously confirmed with current Meta engineers, the social media giant discontinued development. It was unclear why Google Chat was chosen; probably because Meta was already using Google Workspace for emails and docs, and Google Chat is free!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>How is Google Chat nearly a year behind Slack in AI capabilities? </span></strong><span>Slack announced adding MCP support in October 2025, and made the feature generally available this February. Meanwhile, Google Chat announced adding MCP support four months later. Today, in September 2026 it’s only in developer preview, not generally available. Meanwhile, Slack has already shipped </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6afc4595-ad9a-4e60-a40c-fca70609aa2e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Slack Code</span></a><span>, a neat interface for AI coding agents to plug into Slack, including making it easy to review code.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>SaaS is definitely not dead when Meta spends $15-20M/year to buy a chat app. </span></strong><span>Meta has around 75,000 employees, and I estimate it spends in the range of $15-20M annually on Slack. But for much less, it could surely assemble a team of three engineers with a bunch of AI tools and a token budget to build something similar.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Well, Meta did similar with Workplace Chat and after 10 years the result was a product that was worse than Slack; indeed, current Meta engineers told me it had worse performance than Google Chat. AI or not, building a product that works seamlessly for tens of thousands of people and continually adding support for the latest new integrations and AI agents, would take more than a few engineers and some AI tools!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If Meta prefers to pay tens of millions for a chat tool, it’s probably unrealistic for smaller companies to build their own chat SaaS solutions. It could be a reminder of how profitable it can be when you’re the best at doing one thing, like Slack is for chat + AI agent integrations.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Layoffs at Uber and PagerDuty</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Unfortunately, layoffs are back:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Uber: 10%</span></strong><span> (3,000 people) let go this week. Managers have been cut to reduce the number of layers, “micro-teams” (where managers have 1-2 reports) were halved, and plenty of software engineers have been dismissed. It may or not be pertinent that there wasn’t a single mention of AI in the layoff announcement; instead, Uber said it had too many layers, and had probably overhired in recent years.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>PagerDuty: 15%</span></strong><span> (170 people). The paging company has been struggling to grow its business for years, while new startups like Rootly, FireHydrant, incident.io </span><em><span>(note: I’m </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ee66fb9b-c240-47d1-a7a6-2785c362d59f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>an investor</span></a><span>)</span></em><span>, and others are eating their lunch. Uber </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0cc3175a-4a1c-46eb-8c34-185748ecaa66?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>dumped</span></a><span> PagerDuty after 12 years over reliability concerns, and moved to a more reliable startup.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Both Uber and PagerDuty are profitable: Uber is generating $9B of profit (net income) on $55B of annual revenue, while PagerDuty generates $185M profit on $495M of revenue. It’s just that business is not growing as much as before; the stock price demands growth of revenue and/or profits. Both companies likely hope to boost profits by reducing costs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s been a while since the wave of layoffs in 2023, but they keep happening at mature tech companies.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Anthropic upsets devs with usage limit “raise” that’s actually the opposite</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Anthropic predictably angered devs by decreasing usage limits, only days after saying the precise opposite. Is this what happens when corporate comms people take over the writing of announcements?</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px Uber experiencing a 9x increase in agent requests this year is a case in point</span></p></li></ol><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Demand for Apple Mac mini & Mac Studio surges on AI</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI companies are buying Mac mini and Mac Studio models like candy because of their powerful M-series processors (M6 or M5 Ultra in the latest ones), and the memory it supports (up to 512GB for Mac Studio and 32/64GB for Mac mini). From </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3c64f902-3d37-4f1b-b368-c1b2d788fc08?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The Information:</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Some AI labs like OpenAI have bought tens of thousands of Mac minis and Mac Studios for the task of reinforcement learning, a technique where the AI learns through trial and error, said people familiar with OpenAI. OpenAI is using these Macs for training computer-use agents and is desperate to acquire more of them, the people said. Anthropic also rents Mac minis from Amazon’s cloud service, Amazon Web Services, people familiar with Anthropic’s efforts said.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some startups are even building out Mac-only cloud services, in anticipation of a future where demand for Apple hardware grows so much that some AI developers will want to run on Macs in data centers rather than locally.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Demand is so big that NVIDIA is starting to see Apple as its biggest competitor for running local AI workloads. Equally amusingly, Apple has no enterprise strategy, nor any engineering teams focused on its biggest customers, despite enterprises being the biggest buyers of Mac minis and Mac Studios.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Typical Apple: build amazing hardware and hope everything else will follow!</span></p><h3 break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>Imagine a bank account with $100. Let’s assume that two separate withdrawal requests of $10 each arrive at the same moment. However, after the two withdrawals are made, the account still ends up $90.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On a purely technical level, both withdrawal requests completed successfully. There was no error. But the account balance is wrong. The remaining balance should have been $80.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On its own, both transactions were correct. Each read the correct balance and performed the correct calculations. And yet, there is a bug. The reason for this bug was the overlap between the two transactions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You might think this type of overlap is a rare condition. However, this is not true. Overlapping transactions are more or less the normal condition in which databases operate. At any given point in time, multiple processes are trying to write something to a database, often on the same set of records. It just takes two of them to collide with each other inside a window of a few milliseconds for these types of bugs to show up.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So how do we handle such bugs?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is what we are going to try to answer in this article. Here’s what we will cover:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Different ways to handle data conflicts</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So he rebuilt that layer first — one platform carrying data across fabs on three continents, with identity, permissions, and audit trails handled once instead of per project. However, the success of any such RAG system depends on the quality of the embedding model (the model that helps translate words into numbers) that is used by the RAG system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider the example where a particular product’s documentation specifies that annual subscriptions can be refunded only within 30 days. A chatbot built using RAG is supposed to answer customer queries based on this support documentation. However, when a customer asks whether a subscription bought 45 days ago can be refunded, the chatbot confidently answers “yes”.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why did the chatbot make a mess of this seemingly simple question?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The answer lies in the behaviour of the embedding model, which is kind of a translator for AI. This model controls the answer-searching process and is different from the language model that generates the actual answer. No matter how good the language model might be, it cannot give correct answers if the embedding model doesn’t do its job properly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we’re going to look at how this embedding model works in an RAG setup and what makes it such a critical part of the system. Here’s what we will cover:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Why a RAG System Searches Before Answering</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A generic language model’s knowledge depends on what it was taught during training. You can’t expect such a model to know about a company’s private documents, policies, or internal source code. It won’t even know about the company’s latest information that might have been published after the model was trained. Technically, it’s quite costly to retrain a language model every time there’s a change in the information.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is where RAG helps. It separates the ability to generate language from finding relevant details from a pool of stored knowledge. While the language model handles the understanding and writing parts, the external knowledge collection contains the actual information that should be used for writing the answers.</span></p><div documents:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: text.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It divides the text into smaller passages known as chunks.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It sends each chunk into an embedding model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It filters and reranks those chunks, placing them inside the language model’s prompt.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Finally, the language model writes an answer using the prompt that was provided.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure from all this is that RAG doesn’t place the entire document collection into the model’s prompt. This is because doing so would exceed the model’s context limit and fill it with irrelevant information. It also increases costs and latency. The retrieval phase, led by the RAG’s embedding model, serves as the selection step, reducing thousands of passages to a small set for the language model to check.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>How Embeddings Make it Possible to Search by Meaning</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An embedding is basically just a list of numbers that represents a piece of text. A real embedding might contain numbers such as 384, 768, 1024, or several thousand numbers.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/d0041822-acb6-4e6d-9ece-202bb7b9b55e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/80859fee-bbe4-4fd9-abf5-8088ebff967b_2408x1366.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":826,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":87156,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/212751164?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F80859fee-bbe4-4fd9-abf5-8088ebff967b_2408x1366.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="312.0192307692308" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!iWE7!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F80859fee-bbe4-4fd9-abf5-8088ebff967b_2408x1366.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These individual numbers don’t have simple labels describing their meanings. You cannot look at a particular value and say that this means “subscription” while another means “refund”. The overall meaning is distributed across the complete vector. Think of the vector as the coordinates of a point in a mathematical space. An embedding model is trained to place text with related meaning near each other within this mathematical vector space.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is how the system can connect a term like “yearly plan” with “annual subscription”. It can also connect complex phrases like “get my money back” with “receive a refund”. In contrast, a keyword search struggles when a question and the document use different words to explain the same concept. But an embedding model tries to compare the ideas present within the text rather than just the vocabulary. Common techniques behind this are cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance. In a nutshell, the goal of an embedding model is to produce a mathematical score that indicates how close two vectors are to each other.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The embedding model often returns the first k results. This is known as top-k retrieval. For example, if k is 5, the retrieval returns the top 5 highest-ranked chunks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Embedding models also support asymmetric retrieval where the query and document have different forms. The query may be a short question. But the matching document is a longer explanatory passage. For example, the query could be something like: “Can an annual subscription be refunded after 6 weeks?” The answer passage is a statement like: “Annual subscriptions can be refunded within 30 days.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An embedding model trained to compare similar sentences may not perform as well as a model that is trained to connect questions with the relevant passages. To summarize, the embedding model defines what the RAG system considers similar.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Why Related Information is not Always the Right Information</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An embedding model is trained to identify semantic similarity. But a RAG system requires something a bit more strict. It needs to find passages that might contain the information needed to answer a specific question. The problem is that a passage can be related to the question without clearly answering it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, a customer asking how long a refund takes might receive a passage explaining who qualifies for the refund. Both these pieces of information concern refunds, but only one talks about the actual processing time. See the diagram below that shows the concept of semantic search space.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/e67f3312-3680-4b15-827f-48deaa6eaa97?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/fc0152b6-129d-4fe4-8e52-551b5119c32a_3194x1778.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":811,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":220264,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/212751164?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffc0152b6-129d-4fe4-8e52-551b5119c32a_3194x1778.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Multiple failure modes can pop up in this situation:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Similar Subject, Different Question: </span></strong><span>The query asks “How long will an approved refund take to arrive?” The retrieved passage says: “Purchases can be refunded within 30 days.” The passage is relevant to refunds but does not answer the timing question.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Same Words, Different Entity: </span></strong><span>The query asks “how can the billing address be changed.” The retrieved passage explains how to change the account’s email address. Both talk about changing account details. But they refer to completely different fields.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Negation: </span></strong><span>Consider the two passages: “Administrators can delete archived projects”, and “Administrators cannot delete archived projects”. Most of the words are identical. This means their embeddings may be close. But as you can see, they have opposite meanings.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Versions and Dates: </span></strong><span>A knowledge base may contain an old policy and its replacement. The text may be almost identical except for a date, limit, or price. Embeddings cannot automatically know which document is authoritative. Metadata filters or version management rules may need to exclude outdated content explicitly.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Numerical Identifiers: </span></strong><span>The two sentences “Annual subscriptions can be refunded within 30 days” and “Annual subscriptions can be refunded within 60 days” are semantically very similar. But there is a difference in one number, which determines the final answer.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Domain-specific Meanings:</span></strong><span> General models can misunderstand special vocabulary. For example, “capture” has one meaning in an ordinary language and a specific meaning in payment processing. Similarly, the word “port” can refer to networking, hardware, or moving software between platforms. The best model for general web text may not be the best model for legal contracts, medical reports, financial documents, or source code.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Multi-part questions: </span></strong><span>A customer may ask multi-part questions. For example, there could be a question like “Can I cancel the subscription, and how long will the refund take?” The answer for this requires at least two passages. One might explain eligibility for cancellation. Another might explain processing time. The model that retrieves only one subject may produce an incomplete answer.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Why a Better Language Model Cannot Repair Bad Retrieval</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In an RAG system, the language model just sees the user’s question and the selected passages. It doesn’t see every document that might have been stored in the vector database.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, if the annual refund policy document is not retrieved, the language model won’t have any idea about the missing information. A more capable language model may recognize that the retrieved information doesn’t contain the answer. This is useful because it can at least choose not to respond with invalid information. However, this failed retrieval scenario also creates several possible outcomes:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The model answers from its general training knowledge.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It incorrectly applies a related passage.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It might invent a plausible rule.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It says that the available information is insufficient.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It combines conflicting passages incorrectly.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A prompt such as “answer only from the supplied documents” can reduce unsupported answers. But it cannot make the correct document magically appear.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is why testing and debugging are so critical during the development of an RAG system. Developers need to inspect retrieved chunks before changing prompts or swapping language models. It takes a lot more time to solve a retrieval problem in the generation phase.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>What Makes an Embedding Model Suitable For a RAG System</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The most important concern when choosing an embedding model should be retrieval performance. The model should be really good at connecting short questions with longer sentences that might contain the answers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The following characteristics matter:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Domain and Vocabulary:</span></strong><span> The model should understand the language used by the documents and users. Testing should include the use of abbreviations, internal product names, technical terms, and so on. If a company calls annual subscriptions “yearly plans” in the UI, but “annual contracts” in their legal documents, the model should be able to connect those expressions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Language Support: </span></strong><span>A multilingual model is critical when documents, queries, or both may use different languages. The model should be able to connect a query in one language with an answer found in another language.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Embedding Dimensions: </span></strong><span>Embedding dimension is the number of values in each stored vector. Larger vectors preserve more information. But size does not guarantee better retrieval. Also, dimensions have a direct impact on raw storage costs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Maximum Input Length: </span></strong><span>A model with a limit of 8192 tokens can embed much longer text than one limited to 512 tokens. But it doesn’t mean each document should become one big chunk. A long chunk might discuss multiple things like refunds, cancellations, billing addresses, and so on. A focused question may match it less precisely than it would match a smaller passage specific to the relevant policy.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Model and Query Speed: </span></strong><span>Indexing speed determines how much time it takes to embed the document collection. Query speed affects every user request. Some important metrics to consider are the number of chunks embedded per second, query-embedding latency, CPU or GPU requirements, memory use, and the cost of running the model. A model that gains a bit of retrieval quality at the cost of a substantial increase in latency may not be the right choice.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Deployment Requirements: </span></strong><span>Embedding dimensions determine the size of each output vector. Model size determines how much memory and computation are needed to run the embedding model. These are key details required to plan for the model’s deployment.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Why Changing the Embedding Model Later Is Expensive</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each embedding model creates its own vector space, which is unique to the particular model. This means that the embeddings produced by Model A have no dependable relationship with the embeddings produced by Model B.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider an example where all document chunks are embedded using Model A. If we suddenly start to embed the incoming questions using Model B, the system will end up comparing vectors from incompatible spaces. It will be like an apples-to-oranges comparison. Even if both models output the same number of dimensions, the numbers can mean very different things.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This means that the entire corpus of documents needs to be re-embedded using Model B. In other words, migrating an embedding model needs a lot more than just running the new model. It involves the following steps:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Generate new vectors for every chunk.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Build a new vector index.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Apply the correct metadata and access permissions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Keep new or modified documents synchronized during the migration.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Test retrieval quality.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Move production searches to the new index.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Retain a rollback path if the new system performs poorly.</span></p></li></ul><div migration process include embedding API charges or GPU time, index-building time, paying for temporary duplicate storage, data transfer costs, evaluation work, and operational risk.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The migration also changes rankings. For example, a model with a higher benchmark score may perform worse on the application’s specific domain terminology. Therefore, application-specific testing is extremely important to make sure that the answer quality has not gone down.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A few design choices can make it safer to implement future changes:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The original chunks should remain the source of truth. A vector database should not be the only place where processed text exists.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Each chunk should have a stable identifier and a content hash. The hash helps determine whether the text changed and needs a new embedding</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Embedding records should include:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Model name</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Model version or revision</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Embedding dimension</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Query and passage format</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Normalization method</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Chunking version</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Creation time</span></p></li></ul></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A new model should receive a new index or vector field. Its embeddings should not be mixed with old embeddings.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To summarize, a safe migration resembles the classic blue-green deployment approach where the old index continues to serve production traffic even as a new index is built in parallel.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To be clear about things, changing the embedding model is just one of the operations that requires a rebuild. Changing the chunking strategy, parser, cleaning rules, prefixes, or stored dimensions may also require the documents to be rebuilt.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>How Matryoshka Embeddings Offer More Control Over Vector Size</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A basic embedding model produces a fixed-size vector. Its dimensions are meant to work together. We cannot delete most of these dimensions without severely reducing the quality of retrieval.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In contrast, a Matryoshka model is trained differently. During training, such a model is configured to produce useful representations at different prefix lengths, such as the first 256, 512, 1024, and full dimensions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While the initial dimensions contain a useful coarse representation, the later dimensions pack more detailed information. For example, in a 1024-dimensional embedding, the first 256 dimensions can contain a useful small representation. Similarly, the first 512 dimensions contain a more detailed representation. At the end, all 1024 dimensions provide a complete representation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are three practical storage designs to support Matryoshka models:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Storing the smaller vector: </span></strong><span>The system creates an embedding. It then keeps the first 256 dimensions and normalizes the shortened vector if needed. Only these dimensions are stored. This reduces the index size and overall search cost. However, the discarded dimensions are gone forever. If we want to migrate the system to a larger dimension, we need to generate the embeddings again.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Storing the full vector with a smaller search representation: </span></strong><span>The system stores the complete vector in secondary storage. But it places a smaller prefix in the fast vector index. This supports future flexibility. We can build a larger index from the stored vectors without the need to rerun the model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Storing smaller and full vectors for two-stage retrieval: </span></strong><span>The system makes a search on the entire corpus using just 256-dimensional vectors (the reduced dimension). It then retrieves the full vectors for the best candidates and compares them precisely. This brings down the cost of the large initial search. But it retains full precision for the shortlisted candidates.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure Matryoshka embeddings don’t solve incompatibility between different models. They mainly help support different usable sizes within a model’s vector space. Switching to another embedding model still requires the entire re-embedding process we talked about earlier.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As we discussed, an RAG system can’t generate a reliably grounded answer unless it first retrieves the details required for that answer. This makes an embedding model the most important part of an RAG setup.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This doesn’t mean that other things are not important. Retrieval quality of the RAG system also depends on various factors such as:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The existence of the correct documents</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How well the parsing process keeps their content intact</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How the documents are divided into chunks</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How versioning is managed</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Metadata filters and their working</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How a reranker improves the candidate list</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Nevertheless, the embedding model remains central because it helps decide which information enters the language model’s context. It acts as the first major relevance decision in a typical RAG pipeline. The key lesson is to choose an embedding model that retrieves the correct evidence for the questions at an acceptable cost and speed.</span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b4674b0a-149a-404c-bbca-6b0afa3d612d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Twitter</span></a><span>. The topic was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d2c10b0a-42b6-4752-ad33-8651646d49c7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>the seniority rollercoaster</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My personal expectations weren’t high back then; the subscription model for newsletters on platforms like Substack was starting to take off, but the focus was strongly on politics, business, and finance. It wasn’t clear if there was any demand for a publication about software engineering, written by a software engineer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I soon found out there was demand that surpassed </span><em><span>all</span></em><span> my expectations – and then some! Fast forward to today; the newsletter has more than 1.1M readers, tens of thousands of paid subscribers, a podcast, and more than 500,000 YouTube subscribers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>But the numbers aren’t the most validating thing for me; that would be the feedback sent in by readers. </span></strong><span>Via email, in DMs, or in-person at events, it’s great to hear how an article or a podcast we published helped someone try a new approach, or to gain confidence that theirs was the right one, or that an article helped convince a team to change things. It also means a lot to learn that The Pragmatic Engineer helps people feel more confident about keeping up in this fast-changing industry.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Thanks again for your support! </span></em><span>It’s the reason why The Pragmatic Engineer is a viable business and a growing publication, and means we can “scale up” our coverage to deliver ever-more detail about how software gets built, today.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today’s issue covers:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Diving deeper, year after year. </span></strong><span>The evolution of the Pragmatic Engineer’s coverage over five years, getting in through the “front door” instead of the “back door” for deepdives, launching the podcast, The Pragmatic Summit, and growing our team.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>What’s next? </span></strong><span>What we’re excited about, the second Pragmatic Summit, and how you can expect us to stay focused on how building software is changing, and the ways that successful engineers, teams, and companies adapt.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Cash-prize writing contest: </span></strong><span>Software is changing faster than ever. Send us your essay about how things are changing for you, for the chance to win cash prizes worth up to $10,000. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/35a2a2e1-5efa-47ed-a0af-2015bf1ecd66?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Read more on how to take part</span></a><span>.</span></p></li></ol><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>1. Diving deeper, year after year</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Pragmatic Engineer was 15 years in the making and not an overnight success; I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f663af13-6f5e-4b39-ae42-a90f355b2366?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>started</span></a><span> to write a blog in 2007 about software development, which was “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/65c76e2b-7847-4b7b-a23f-03b7579b125d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>rebooted</span></a><span>” as “The Pragmatic Engineer Blog” in 2015. At the time, it was read by almost nobody! </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b7867433-c79d-478b-a629-fc4d351b0c47?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>In 2019</span></a><span>, I launched an email digest (“v0” of the newsletter), and a year later, I decided to focus on the newsletter fulltime after quitting Uber as a manager following job cuts in 2020, when a quarter of my team was laid off and the rest were disbanded due to the pandemic. I took an employment break, planning to finish </span><em><span>‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce26b6d4-2b75-4cbc-ab40-612f58cee120?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The Software Engineer’s Guidebook</span></a><span>’</span></em><span> in six months and then start a VC-funded startup. In the end, finishing the book took another two years, and I didn’t kick off that VC-funded startup! Instead, I decided to go all-in on writing a newsletter targeted exclusively at software engineers and engineering leaders.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position:
